### Summary

If you pass `--keep-stage-std` to e.g. `x build`, and the std of that stage hasn't been built yet, the command fails. This means that, in order to use the flag, one needs to remember to remove it from the first invocation of the command, and add it to all the subsequent ones. It would be nicer if one could just use the flag in all invocations, and have `x` do the right thing (build std if absent, keep if present)

### Command used

```sh
x clean
x build --stage 2 --keep-stage-std 1 compiler
```

### Expected behaviour

std is built, and the compilation continues

### Actual behaviour

```
Building stage1 compiler artifacts (stage0 -> stage1, x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu)
    Finished `release` profile [optimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 1.06s
Creating a sysroot for stage1 compiler (use `rustup toolchain link 'name' build/host/stage1`)
Building stage1 lld-wrapper (stage0 -> stage1, x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu)
    Finished `release` profile [optimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 0.20s
WARNING: Using a potentially old libstd. This may not behave well.
ERROR: Unable to find the stamp file [REDACTED]/build/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/stage1-std/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/dist/.libstd-stamp, did you try to keep a nonexistent build stage?
Build completed unsuccessfully in 0:00:02
```

### Bootstrap configuration (bootstrap.toml)
```toml
profile = "compiler"  # Includes one of the default files in src/bootstrap/defaults
change-id = 162423

[rust]
deny-warnings = false
debug-logging = true
```

### Operating system

NixOS 26.11

### HEAD

8a9dd7abdf013ec10cfeaaa3685feba18ef1c90c

### Additional context

The same probably applies to `--keep-stage`, but I basically don't use it and so can't give a nice example of use

<!--
Thank you for filing a bug report! 🐛 Please provide a short summary of the bug,
along with any information you feel relevant to replicating the bug.
-->

`musl` drops `O_PATH` because the corresponding flag is defined as an access mode and dropped with the read/write etc. See the repro:

```rust
use std::{fs::OpenOptions, io::Read, os::unix::fs::OpenOptionsExt};

fn main() {
    let mut f = OpenOptions::new()
        .read(true)
        .custom_flags(0o10000000) // libc::O_PATH (x86_64)
        .open(std::env::current_exe().unwrap())
        .unwrap();
    // An O_PATH fd cannot be read, so this must fail with EBADF.
    let r = f.read(&mut [0; 1]);
    assert!(r.is_err());
}
```



Works with `gnu`:
```
rustc repro.rs --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu  && ./repro
```

Panics with `musl`:
```
rustc repro.rs --target x86_64-unknown-linux-musl  && ./repro

thread 'main' (224730) panicked at repro.rs:11:5:
assertion failed: r.is_err()
note: run with `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` environment variable to display a backtrace
```

The reason for this seem to be `custom_flags` setting `O_ACCMODE`.  
In [musl here](https://git.musl-libc.org/cgit/musl/tree/include/fcntl.h): 
```c
#define O_SEARCH   O_PATH
#define O_EXEC     O_PATH
#define O_TTY_INIT 0

#define O_ACCMODE (03|O_SEARCH)
```

vs [glibc](https://codebrowser.dev/glibc/glibc/sysdeps/unix/sysv/linux/bits/fcntl-linux.h.html#_M/O_ACCMODE):
```c
#define O_ACCMODE	   0003
```

I tried this code:

```rust
// Expected output "A"; at -O (opt-level >= 2) it prints "B".
#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord, Debug)]
pub enum K { A, B, C }

pub enum E { Leaf(K), Wrap(Box<E>) }

impl E {
    pub fn kind(&self) -> K {
        match self {
            E::Leaf(k) => *k,
            E::Wrap(e) => std::cmp::max(K::B, e.kind()),
        }
    }
}

pub fn f(e: &E) -> K {
    match e.kind() {
        K::C => K::B,
        k => k,
    }
}

fn main() {
    let e = E::Leaf(K::A);
    println!("{:?}", f(&e));
}

body_text:
This issue was found by an LLM after I asked it to audit some trait implementations of `Path` and related types.

I tried this code:

```rust
use std::path::Path;

fn main() {
    let mut drive = Path::new("C:").components();
    drive.next(); // consumes the Disk prefix
    
    let mut unc = Path::new(r"\\server\share").components();
    unc.next(); // consumes the UNC prefix
    
    println!("{}", PartialEq::eq(&drive, &unc));
    println!("{:?}", Ord::cmp(&drive, &unc));
}
```

On a windows machine, this outputs:

```
true
Less
```

This violates the laws documented for `PartialOrd`/`Ord`. The docs [state](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/cmp/trait.Ord.html):
> exactly one of `a < b`, `a == b` or `a > b` is true

Related issues: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/164470, https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/164467 and https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/164415

body_text:
I ran the following python script, which runs rustc with a non-UTF-8 input file name:

```python
import subprocess

p = subprocess.run(["rustc", bytes([255])], check=False)
print(p)
```

I got the following output (the empty line is not a copy-paste error):

```

thread 'main' (468943) panicked at /rustc/b6eeb93c992027a03e1fd120b6652546396b142c/library/std/src/env.rs:935:51:
called `Result::unwrap()` on an `Err` value: "\xFF"
note: run with `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` environment variable to display a backtrace
CompletedProcess(args=['rustc', b'\xff'], returncode=101)
```

If I instead set `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` before running the script, I get the following output (again, the empty line is not a copy-paste error. And for this one, in my terminal, the error message is bolded and has color):

```
error: argument 1 is not valid Unicode: "\xFF"

CompletedProcess(args=['rustc', b'\xff'], returncode=1)
```

Seems like whatever is trying to output the error message doesn't like it when `RUST_BACKTRACE` isn't set. (Also note that the `returncode` in the two outputs are different.)

# ReferencePropagation incorrectly increases alignment of raw field loads

### I tried this code

```rust
#[repr(C, align(8))]
pub struct Aligned8 {
    field: u32,
}

#[unsafe(no_mangle)]
pub fn raw_field_read(input: &[u64; 2]) -> u32 {
    unsafe {
        let ptr = input.as_ptr().cast::<u8>().add(4).cast::<Aligned8>();
        let field = &raw const (*ptr).field;
        field.read()
    }
}
```

Compile with:

```bash
rustc +nightly-2026-10-11 --edition=2024 --crate-type=lib \
  -C opt-level=3 --emit=llvm-ir -o enabled.ll repro.rs
```

Then disable `ReferencePropagation`:

```bash
rustc +nightly-2026-10-11 --edition=2024 --crate-type=lib \
  -C opt-level=3 -Zmir-enable-passes=-ReferencePropagation \
  --emit=llvm-ir -o disabled.ll repro.rs
```

### I expected to see this happen

The pointer is offset by four bytes from an eight-byte-aligned address. It is properly aligned for the `u32` field, but not for the `Aligned8` aggregate.

The raw field pointer is valid to construct, and the subsequent read dereferences a properly aligned `*const u32`.

According to the [[Rust Reference](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/behavior-considered-undefined.html#places-based-on-misaligned-pointers)](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/behavior-considered-undefined.html#places-based-on-misaligned-pointers), the alignment requirement depends on the pointer dereferenced by the last `*` projection.

The generated LLVM load should therefore use `align 4`.

### Instead, this happened

With `ReferencePropagation` enabled:

```llvm
%_0 = load i32, ptr %_3, align 8, !noundef !5
```

With `ReferencePropagation` disabled:

```llvm
%_0 = load i32, ptr %_3, align 4, !noundef !5
```

The relevant MIR transformation is effectively:

```diff
- _field = &raw const ((*_ptr).0: u32);
- _0 = copy (*_field);
+ _0 = copy ((*_ptr).0: u32);
```

The local names are illustrative.

This changes the final dereference from a properly aligned `*const u32` to a misaligned `*const Aligned8` field projection, introducing an unjustified alignment assumption and potentially undefined behavior.

The issue reproduces on both stable Rust 1.98.1 and nightly Rust 1.101.0.

I tried this code:

```rust
pub fn test() -> impl Fn() -> bool {
   let i = &42u8;
   || &42u8 == i
}
```

It expectedly failed to compile:

```
error[E0373]: closure may outlive the current function, but it borrows `i`, which is owned by the current function
 --> src/lib.rs:3:4
  |
3 |    || &42u8 == i
  |    ^^          - `i` is borrowed here
  |    |
  |    may outlive borrowed value `i`
  |
note: closure is returned here
 --> src/lib.rs:3:4
  |

  |    ^^^^^^^^^^^^^
help: to force the closure to take ownership of `i` (and any other referenced variables), use the `move` keyword
  |
3 |    move || &42u8 == i
  |    ++++
```

Then, I tried this code (on edition 2021+):

```rust
pub fn test() -> impl Fn() -> bool {
   let i = &42u8;
   || &42u8 <= i
}

It incorrectly compiled!

It seems that the `PartialEq` operators work one way, and the `PartialOrd` ones another.

body_text:
The following code doesn't compile, when compiled as a binary crate:

```rust
#[track_caller]
fn foo() {}

use foo as main;
```

Error output:
```
error: `main` function is not allowed to be `#[track_caller]`
 --> src/main.rs:1:1
  |
1 | #[track_caller]
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ help: remove this annotation
2 | fn foo() {}
  | -------- `main` function is not allowed to be `#[track_caller]`

error: could not compile `playground` (bin "playground") due to 1 previous error
```

Removing the `#[track_caller]` makes the code compile.

Since `foo` might be defined in a different crate, this means that it is technically a semver breakage to add `#[track_caller]` to any public function whose signature is compatible with `main`. This seems undesirable.

See also: https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/213817-t-lang/topic/Should.20using.20.60track_caller.60.20.2B.20.60no_mangle.60.20be.20disallowed.3F/with/631453944

_Noticed when looking at https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/164589_

On type mismatch on resolved associated functions, we currently output a diagnostic like the following:

```
[INFO] [stdout] error[E0308]: mismatched types
[INFO] [stdout]   --> src/main.rs:29:3
[INFO] [stdout]    |
[INFO] [stdout] 28 |     let mut nns: Vec<NeuralNetwork> = Vec::from_fn(
[INFO] [stdout]    |                                       ------------ arguments to this function are incorrect
[INFO] [stdout] 29 |         NUMBER_OF_NNS as u32,
[INFO] [stdout]    |         ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ expected `usize`, found `u32`
[INFO] [stdout]    |
[INFO] [stdout] note: associated function defined here
[INFO] [stdout]   --> /rustc/e3feeb59cd1bdd011a2bfcc0747b55125d9b8527/library/alloc/src/vec/mod.rs:795:11
[INFO] [stdout] help: you can convert a `u32` to a `usize` and panic if the converted value doesn't fit
[INFO] [stdout]    |
[INFO] [stdout] 29 |         (NUMBER_OF_NNS as u32).try_into().unwrap(),
[INFO] [stdout]    |         +                    +++++++++++++++++++++
```

although serviceable, this diagnostic doesn't account that there's a *different* `from_fn` available for `Vec` (in that project) for which the params would have been correct. Ideally we'd provide a structured suggestion, but at the very least, when we've got enough information to point "arguments to this function are incorrect", it would be nice to look for other functions with the same/similar name within the same module/type (like detecting that `foo::from_fn` should have been `foo::try_from_fn` or `foo::from_fn_in`).

I'd love to have some way to automatically write ``[\`rustc::TyCtxt\`]`` in a Github text box and link the actual `TyCtxt` struct automatically. So, having some way to run the search results server-side, and then redirect to the search result.
I know that this could cause problems if structs change names, but that already happens.

body_text:
Today I learned that in the x86-64 SysV ABI, ["a [..] global array variable of length at least 16 bytes … always has alignment of at least 16 bytes."](https://gitlab.com/x86-psABIs/x86-64-ABI/-/blob/master/x86-64-ABI/low-level-sys-info.tex#L323)

This is an additional alignment requirement separate from the type's alignment.  Yes, this applies to variables specifically of array type, not any other type even if it contains an array.

On Windows AArch64, there is a somewhat saner version of this: [all global variables are aligned](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/cpp/build/arm64-windows-abi-conventions?view=msvc-170#alignment) to an alignment depending on their size.  For example, variables of size >= 64 are aligned to 16.

[According to Clang](https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/blob/15354062581dab747d2f931f13a7b188bfec0112/clang/lib/Basic/TargetInfo.cpp#L1151), Windows x86-64 does the same but this is not documented.

In each of these cases (even the undocumented one!), Clang demands this alignment.  If you write:
```cpp
extern unsigned char x[64], y[64];
void copy() {
    __builtin_memcpy(x, y, 64);
}
```
then on all the aforementioned (but not other targets), [Clang emits](https://gcc.godbolt.org/z/5r5vTTcrT) LLVM IR with `align 16`:
```
@x = external local_unnamed_addr global [16 x i32], align 16
@y = external local_unnamed_addr global [16 x i32], align 16
```
This causes UB if the variables are not so aligned.  In practice on x86-64 this means that `movaps` instructions get emitted instead of `movups` instructions.  

However, rustc seems to not know about these rules.  AFAIU, the following should be guaranteed to be compatible with the above C declaration:

```rust
#[unsafe(no_mangle)]
pub static mut x: [u8; 64] = [1; 64];
```

It doesn't say `extern "C"`, but there is no way to use `extern "C"` with exported statics.  The type `[u8; 64]` is FFI-safe.

But [rustc produces](https://rust.godbolt.org/z/d3Mj8a8av) LLVM IR with only `align 1` on all of these targets.

Note: I also tested the C sample on GCC (x86-64 Linux) and MSVC (x86-64 Windows) and they both use `movups` instead of `movaps`, indicating that they don't make this assumption about imports, although they should still properly align exports.  I didn't check AArch64 as it doesn't have an obvious assembly-level distinction and I don't know how to dig into those compilers' IRs.

body_text:
We found this in our monorepo in a mixed C++/Rust setting, but with some persistence and a little bit of LLMs, we've got a reproducer that doesn't need any C++: https://github.com/durin42/rust/commit/hwasan-lto-backwards-reference

The rough summary is this: hwasan needs to emit some references (eg `@__hwasan_personality_thunk`) that resolve in the hwasan support library at link time. Crate-level LTO _can_ sometimes turn the reference into an external declaration, and then depending on the order objects get loaded by the linker you can get backwards references (which our setup treats as errors.)

Based on #164705

Exhibit A: https://godbolt.org/z/9qsj19Yo3
```rust
struct A(Box<A>);

fn main() {
    let x: A;
    _ = x.0.0.0.0.0; // dereference whatever we find on the stack at this point, repeatedly
}
```
output:
```shell
> cargo run -q

thread 'main' (1836790) panicked at src/main.rs:5:9:
null pointer dereference occurred
note: run with `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` environment variable to display a backtrace
thread caused non-unwinding panic. aborting.
Job 1, 'cargo run -q' terminated by signal SIGABRT (Abort)
```
May instead exit with SIGSEGV or stack overflow (which is printed by the SIGSEGV handler), depending on the weather (all on linux).
(Presumably because the garbage we read as pointers here depends on the system)

----

Exhibit B: https://godbolt.org/z/sW6EMrPss
```rust 
struct A(Box<A>);

fn main() {
    let a = std::hint::black_box(1);
    let b = std::hint::black_box(1);

    assert_eq!(a, b);

    let x: A; // LLVM sees the UB here and marks the non-panicking branch of the assert unreachable
    let _ = x.0.0;
}
```
output:
```shell
> RUSTFLAGS='-Zmir-opt-level=0' cargo +nightly run --release -q

thread 'main' (1838663) panicked at src/main.rs:7:5:
assertion `left == right` failed
  left: 1
 right: 1
note: run with `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` environment variable to display a backtrace
```
-----
Exhibit C: https://godbolt.org/z/ehdrKMzPx
```rust
fn main() {
    let x = Box::new(Box::new(Box::new(Box::new(Box::new(Box::new(1))))));
    drop(x);
    _ = ******x; // dereference whatever garbage the global allocator leaves behind in the box(es)
}
```
output:
```sh
> cargo run -q

thread 'main' (1906552) panicked at src/main.rs:4:9:
misaligned pointer dereference: address must be a multiple of 0x8 but is 0x62e0d41b8912
note: run with `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` environment variable to display a backtrace
thread caused non-unwinding panic. aborting.
Job 1, 'cargo run -q' terminated by signal SIGABRT (Abort)
```
or if the pointer happens to be aligned:
```sh
> cargo run -q
Job 1, 'cargo run -q' terminated by signal SIGSEGV (Address boundary error)
```

body_text:
Clang and msvc only pass the first 3 vector arguments in SSE registers, and additional vectors are passed indirectly

https://godbolt.org/z/4dT4vveoY
https://godbolt.org/z/s8vsM8Yvs

It's easiest to see this in the IR. Clang adds the `inreg` attribute to the vectors, but that isn't really needed, because LLVM will use registers anyway. But for the fourth vector argument, rust just uses `<16 x i8>` while clang uses `ptr`.

---

Fixing this is tricker than it seems. Vectorcall actually gets 6 vector registers, so we need to distinguish fastcall and vectorcall. 

But the most annoying bit is that the size of the arguments is used in the name mangling, and when rust just gives a `ptr` argument to LLVM (these are untyped these days) the size calculation is off. Clang circumvents this by doing the calculation itself. We'd need to do this too.

Alternatively we can see if we can get LLVM to hook up `byref` into their mangling calculation.

---

All of this is a bit of a hassle for a very old target. Apparently nobody uses more than 3 simd vectors in C FFI there. Still, we probably should fix this. I was looking into this code due to [`-Zregparm`](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/131749), adding it on a shaky foundation is extra challenging.

---

Fixing this is tricker than it seems. Vectorcall actually gets 6 vector registers, so we need to distinguish fastcall and vectorcall.

Alternatively we can see if we can get LLVM to hook up `byref` into their mangling calculation.

---

### Summary

Currently, `wildcard_enum_match_arm` will indicate against using a wildcard
even in the case that the wildcard is marked as `unreachable!()`.

I find this a little too noisy.
Sometimes, instead of matching enums by explicitly stating all variants,
it can be more readable to group some variants under a method of the form `is_*()`
or use any kind of `if` guard.
When using guards, the use of unreachable wildcards is usually necessary and useful.

The `unreachable!()` macro is enough to catch any bugs that may hide in the guards,
given an extensive enough test suite.

### Lint Name

wildcard_enum_match_arm

### Reproducer

I tried this code:

```rust
let lval = match left.kind() {
    wir::Kind::ConstInt(i) => i64::try_from(i).unwrap(),
    wir::Kind::ConstSigned(s) => s,
    x if !x.is_number() => return None,
    _ => unreachable!(),
};

```

I saw this happen:

```
206 |         _ => unreachable!(),
    |         ^ help: try: `x @ wir::Kind::Return | x @ wir::Kind::Neg ...
```

I expected to see this happen:

No warning at all.
If more variants are added that do not fall in the filter
(in this case we only care about numbers),
the unreachable!() will panic, so no lint is necessary.

### Version

### Summary

When a `-Ctarget-cpu` option is passed to rustc, certain `is_x86_feature_detected!` invocations become compile-time constants. Clippy flags this code with `clippy::assertions_on_constants`, despite the constantness of the expression being dependent on the build configuration.

### Lint Name

assertions_on_constants

### Reproducer

I tried this code:

```rust
fn main() {
    assert!(std::arch::is_x86_feature_detected!("sse4.2"));
}
```

By default, no clippy assertion is issued (which is correct). If you then add the following to `.cargo/config.toml`:

```
[target.'cfg(target_arch = "x86_64")']
rustflags = ["-Ctarget-cpu=x86-64-v2"]
```

This now occurs
```
warning: this assertion has a constant value
 --> src/main.rs:2:5
  |
2 |     assert!(std::arch::is_x86_feature_detected!("sse4.2"));
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  |
  = help: consider moving this into a const block: `const { assert!(..) }`
  = help: for further information visit https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-clippy/rust-1.92.0/index.html#assertions_on_constants
  = note: `#[warn(clippy::assertions_on_constants)]` on by default
```

Further note that following the suggestion fails:
```
error[E0015]: cannot call non-const function `std_detect::detect::arch::x86::__is_feature_detected::sse4_2` in constants
 --> src/main.rs:2:21
  |
2 |     const { assert!(std::arch::is_x86_feature_detected!("sse4.2")) };
  |                     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  |
  = note: calls in constants are limited to constant functions, tuple structs and tuple variants
  = note: this error originates in the macro `std::arch::is_x86_feature_detected` (in Nightly builds, run with -Z macro-backtrace for more info)

For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0015`.
error: could not compile `tmp-warning` (bin "tmp-warning") due to 1 previous error
```

### Version

rustc 1.92.0 (ded5c06cf 2025-12-08)

When a `-Ctarget-cpu` option is passed to rustc, certain `is_x86_feature_detected!` invocations become compile-time constants. Clippy flags this code with `clippy::assertions_on_constants`, despite the constantness of the expression being dependent on the build configuration.

### Lint Name

assertions_on_constants

### Reproducer

I tried this code:

```rust
fn main() {
    assert!(std::arch::is_x86_feature_detected!("sse4.2"));
}
```

By default, no clippy assertion is issued (which is correct). If you then add the following to `.cargo/config.toml`:

```
[target.'cfg(target_arch = "x86_64")']
rustflags = ["-Ctarget-cpu=x86-64-v2"]
```

  = note: `#[warn(clippy::assertions_on_constants)]` on by default
```

### Summary

Using a "complex" `cfg` attribute like `#[cfg(all(test))]` on a module that contains a function with the `test` attribute causes `tests_outside_test_module` to incorrectly fire. In my case I know the tests in the module will `panic` due to OOM when using a 16-bit architecture since more than `i16::MAX` bytes is needed, so my actual example was using `#[cfg(all(test, not(target_pointer_width = "16")))]`.

### Lint Name

tests_outside_test_module

### Reproducer

I tried this code:

```rust
#[deny(clippy::tests_outside_test_module, reason = "example")]
#[expect(clippy::non_minimal_cfg, reason = "example")]
#[cfg(all(test))]
mod tests {
    #[test]
    fn foo() {}
}
```

I saw this happen:

```bash
error: this function marked with #[test] is outside a #[cfg(test)] module
 --> src/lib.rs:6:5
  |
6 |     fn foo() {}
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^
  |
  = note: move it to a testing module marked with #[cfg(test)]
  = help: for further information visit https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-clippy/rust-1.93.0/index.html#tests_outside_test_module
  = note: example
note: the lint level is defined here
 --> src/lib.rs:1:8
  |
1 | #[deny(clippy::tests_outside_test_module, reason = "example")]
  |        ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

error: could not compile `example` (lib test) due to 1 previous error
```

I expected to see this happen: no lints to fire

### Version

### What it does

Usually `cdylib` crates are for dynamic loading into existing processes. When these `dylib`s are unloaded (yes i know it's a niche use case and its os-dependent caveats), the drop glues and drop impls for the statics are NOT executed, which might cause surprises.

A lint can help spotting these statics item (which might be hidden deep inside the dependency tree), and helps properly handle them with crates like `dtor`.

### Advantage

_No response_

### Drawbacks

_No response_

### Example
```rust
static HUGE_BUFFER: LazyLock<Vec<u8>> = LazyLock::new(|| {
    load_data_from_filesystem()
});
```

body_text: ### Summary When the `missing_inline_in_public_items` lint is enabled in a proc macro crate, if the exported proc macro `fn` item is not annotated with `#[inline]`, the lint triggers sometimes but not always. In my case, rust-analyzer for VSCode does show the lint being triggered, but the CLI does not. ### Lint Name missing_inline_in_public_items ### Reproducer I tried this code: ```rust #![deny(clippy::missing_inline_in_public_items)] use proc_macro::TokenStream; #[proc_macro_derive(Error, attributes(display))] pub fn impl_error(input: TokenStream) -> TokenStream { input } ``` ...in a proc macro crate: ```toml [package] name = "rust-playground" version = "0.1.0" edition = "2024" [lib] proc-macro = true [dependencies] ``` I got this output from the CLI (no errors): ``` ➜ rust-playground git:(master) ✗ cargo clippy Checking rust-playground v0.1.0 (/Users/luisferlcc/rust-playground) Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 0.13s ``` ...but this output from rust-analyzer (error): I expected to see the same result from the CLI and from rust-analyzer, preferably that neither trigger the lint, since `#[inline]` doesn't make much sense for a proc macro. ### Version ```text rustc 1.93.0 (254b59607 2026-01-19) binary: rustc commit-hash: 254b59607d4417e9dffbc307138ae5c86280fe4c commit-date: 2026-01-19 host: aarch64-apple-darwin release: 1.93.0 LLVM version: 21.1.8 ``` ### Additional Labels @rustbot label +L-restriction @rustbot label +T-macros

### Description

I like the idea of `absolute_paths` but my heuristic I generally use is if something is used once or twice can remain as an absolute path.

Namely, support impls that are gated by `#[cfg(feature = "")] impl MyCrateTrait for some::foreign::Type {}`. Especially with a large workspace, specifying the allowed crate prefixes means that all occurrences of this type workspace-wide will now get excluded by the rule, or I have to do an `#[expect()]` attribute on all of them.

What I'd _really_ like is to specify `absolute-paths-max-occurrences = 2` in my `clippy.toml` to say "if this absolute path is used more than twice in a given file, it should trigger an `absolute_paths` warning".

### Summary

`manual_clamp` doesn't trigger if one of the bounds being used is the return value from a function.

Applying this lint might change the meaning of the code if a function returns different results successive times it's called, but I think for a `MaybeIncorrect` lint it's reasonable to suggest this at least in cases where the function takes no mutable references and is given the same arguments.

### Lint Name

manual_clamp

### Reproducer

I tried [this code](https://play.rust-lang.org/?version=stable&mode=debug&edition=2024&gist=b135de777aed1d25b8701db738279827):

```rust
fn upper_bound() -> f32 {
    5.0
}

pub fn manual_clamp(f: f32) -> f32 {
    if f < 0. { 0. } else if f > upper_bound() { upper_bound() } else { f }
}
```

I expected to see the `manual_clamp` lint trigger on the `manual_clamp` function.

Instead, this happened:

No lints

### Summary

Macros generally shouldn't trigger lints in code they generate (#407). But I've found that if I use `implicit_return = "deny"` and a macro generates that code on an `async fn` this lint triggers. The `async` part causes the `#[tracing::instrument]` macro to generate different code than synchronous, so it's possible `async` isn't relevant to clippy, but I figure I'd mention it explicitly just in case.

### Lint Name

implicit_return

### Reproducer

I tried this code:

**Cargo.toml:**

```
[package]
name = "clippy-implicit-return-instrument-repro"
edition = "2024"

[dependencies]
tracing = { version = "0.1.44", features = ["attributes"] }

[lints.clippy]
implicit_return = "deny"
```

**src/lib.rs:**

```rust
#[tracing::instrument]
pub async fn run() {
}
```

I saw this happen:

```
error: missing `return` statement
 --> src/lib.rs:1:1
  |
1 | #[tracing::instrument]
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  |
  = help: for further information visit https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-clippy/rust-1.94.0/index.html#implicit_return
  = note: requested on the command line with `-D clippy::implicit-return`
  = note: this error originates in the attribute macro `tracing::instrument` (in Nightly builds, run with -Z macro-backtrace for more info)
```

I expected to see this happen:

Lint should not fire in macro-generated code (see #407).

### Summary

### Summary

When type inferencing infers the type of some numeric literal to be the same as the numeric fallback type (`i32` or `f64`), a warning is incorrectly emitted as though it fell back to being that type. This is especially bad when using macros to write generics over numeric types as you cannot specify the type (at least not in any way that's more ergonomic than adding an `allow`).


### Lint Name

default_numeric_fallback

### Reproducer

### Reproducer

```rust
#![warn(clippy::default_numeric_fallback)]
let a = 92i32;
// will warn on any operation between `a` and a literal, e.g.
let _ = a + 3;
// note `literal << a` and `literal >> a` should warn.

let b = 92f64;
// will warn on any operation between `b` and a literal, e.g.
let _ = b + 3.0;
```

I expected to see this happen:
No warnings emitted.

### What it does

I finally discovered today, after extensive trial and error, and after consulting JetBrains Junie before finally noticing the answer in a Google Gemini response, that the reason RustRover was failing to load my benchmark package's dependencies from `benches/Cargo.toml` was that it was expecting their source code to be in `benches/src/benchmarks.rs` rather than `benches/benchmarks.rs`, which is where I had it.

### Advantage

- Make it much easier to use all kinds of tools in multi-Cargo.toml workspaces.
- Eliminate guesswork about seemingly-likely solutions that don't work (e.g. moving the benchmarks' dependencies from `[dependencies]` to `[dev-dependencies]`.

### Drawbacks

May need some exclusion rules to deal with Cargo.toml's that are specifically adapted to being siblings of the *.rs files in the directory tree rather than uncles via `./src`.

### Example

```sh
$ ls -r
Cargo.toml
benches

benches/
Cargo.toml
benchmarks.rs
```

In Cargo.toml:
```toml
[workspace]
members = [
    ".",        # The main crate in the current directory
    "benches",  # The new benchmark-only crate
]
```

In benches/Cargo.toml:
```toml
[[bench]]
name = "benchmarks"
path = "benchmarks.rs"
```

Could be written as:

```sh
$ ls -r
Cargo.toml
benches

benches/
Cargo.toml
src

benches/src/
benchmarks.rs
```

In benches/Cargo.toml:
```
[[bench]]
name = "benchmarks"
path = "src/benchmarks.rs"
```

### Comparison with existing lints

AFAICT no lints currently evaluate the directory structure of a workspace.

### What it does

Like `missing_inline_in_public_items`, but with no regards for visibility.


### Advantage

It is much easier to silence a warning rather than notice that some non-`pub` function,
that is immediately called by a public function was forgotten to be marked as `#[inline]`,
just because one got used to lints from `missing_inline_in_public_items`, and didn't think about it.

### Drawbacks

This would perhaps be a restriction-type of lint, one that is stylistic in nature.

### Example

```
fn foo() {} // missing #[inline]
fn bar() {} // missing #[inline]
fn baz() { bar(); } // missing #[inline]
```

### Comparison with existing lints

There is `missing_inline_in_public_items`, but it only applies to `pub` items.

## Summary

Clippy panics with an internal compiler error due to unstable fingerprints in incremental compilation when checking code that uses `futures_util` stream combinators (`filter_map` + `buffer_unordered` + `collect`) with async closures.

## Version

```
rustc 1.95.0 (59807616e 2026-04-14)
clippy 0.1.95 (59807616e1 2026-04-14)
x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
```

## Error output

```
error: internal compiler error: encountered incremental compilation error with evaluate_obligation(756fcc40b4fb2203-2f9389f8417c9990)
  |
  = note: please follow the instructions below to create a bug report with the provided information
  = note: for incremental compilation bugs, having a reproduction is vital

thread 'rustc' panicked at compiler/rustc_middle/src/verify_ich.rs:80:9:
Found unstable fingerprints for evaluate_obligation(756fcc40b4fb2203-2f9389f8417c9990): Ok(EvaluatedToOk)
```

## Query stack during panic

```
#0 [evaluate_obligation] evaluating trait selection obligation `{async closure@src/fs/watcher.rs:712:17: 712:34}: futures_util::fns::FnMut1<core::option::Option<(String, PathBuf, u64, SystemTime)>>`
#1 [type_op_ascribe_user_type] evaluating `type_op_ascribe_user_type` (StreamExt::collect with FilterMap<BufferUnordered<Iter<Map<IntoIter<String>, CoroutineClosure>>>, CoroutineClosure>)
... and 13 other queries
```

## Dep node stack (try_mark_green)

```
#0 check_match(backend_rs::create_app_from_endpoint)
#1 mir_built(backend_rs::create_app_from_endpoint)
#2 has_ffi_unwind_calls(backend_rs::create_app_from_endpoint)
#3 mir_promoted(backend_rs::create_app_from_endpoint)
#4 mir_borrowck(backend_rs::create_app_from_endpoint)
```

## Reproduction notes

- Occurs during **incremental compilation** only. A clean build (`cargo clean -p backend-rs`) succeeds.
- The code uses `futures_util` stream combinators: `buffer_unordered` → `filter_map` (with an async closure) → `collect::<Vec<_>>()`.
- Compiler flags: `--crate-type lib -C embed-bitcode=no -C debuginfo=2 -C incremental=[REDACTED]`
- Triggered by `cargo clippy -- -D warnings` on a subsequent build after source changes.

## Workaround

`cargo clean -p backend-rs` clears the corrupted incremental cache and allows compilation to succeed.

### What it does

As per title, for projects with MSRV 1.82 or higher:
- Suggest replacing `addr_of!(x)` with `&raw const x`
- Suggest replacing `addr_of_mut!(x)` with `&raw mut x`

### Advantage

The macros are [documented](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/ptr/macro.addr_of.html) as soft-deprecated; seems like encouraging use of the operators would fit that recommendation.

### Drawbacks

_No response_

### Example

```rust
addr_of!(x);
addr_of_mut!(y);
```

Could be written as:

```rust
&raw const x;
&raw mut y;
```


### Comparison with existing lints

_No response_

### Additional Context

_No response_

### Summary

`unnecessary_cast` suppresses casts of values whose type might be a cfg-dependent type alias (e.g. libc struct fields) by conservatively skipping when the cast source involves an external function it can't inspect. But that suppression only matches *free* functions (`Res::Def(DefKind::Fn, _)` on a path expr), so two semantically equivalent initializations of the same local lint differently: initializing via `std::mem::zeroed()` suppresses the lint, while initializing via `MaybeUninit::uninit()` + `.assume_init()` does not — `assume_init` is a method call (no callee path expr) and `MaybeUninit::uninit` resolves to `DefKind::AssocFn`, which the check doesn't match.

The cast in the reproducer is genuinely platform-dependent (`statvfs.f_blocks` is `fsblkcnt_t`, not `u64` on every target), so the lint's own rationale for the alias suppression applies equally to both forms. The practical effect is that migrating FFI out-params from `mem::zeroed()` to the more idiomatic `MaybeUninit` surfaces this false positive and forces an `#[allow]`.

### Lint Name

unnecessary_cast

### Reproducer

I tried this code (with `libc = "0.2"`, on x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu):

```rust
fn with_zeroed(path: &std::ffi::CStr) -> u64 {
    let mut s: libc::statvfs = unsafe { std::mem::zeroed() };
    unsafe { libc::statvfs(path.as_ptr(), &mut s) };
    s.f_blocks as u64
}

fn with_maybe_uninit(path: &std::ffi::CStr) -> u64 {
    let mut s = std::mem::MaybeUninit::<libc::statvfs>::uninit();
    unsafe { libc::statvfs(path.as_ptr(), s.as_mut_ptr()) };
    let s = unsafe { s.assume_init() };
    s.f_blocks as u64
}
```

I expected to see this happen: both functions treated the same — no lint on either, since `f_blocks` is the cfg-dependent alias `fsblkcnt_t` and the cast is required on targets where it isn't `u64`.

Instead, this happened: only the `MaybeUninit` version lints:

```
warning: casting to the same type is unnecessary (`u64` -> `u64`)
  --> src/main.rs:11:5
   |
11 |     s.f_blocks as u64
   |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ help: try: `s.f_blocks`
```

The cast in the reproducer is genuinely platform-dependent (`statvfs.f_blocks` is `fsblkcnt_t`, not `u64` on every target), so the lint's own rationale for the alias suppression applies equally to both forms. The practical effect is that migrating FFI out-params from `mem::zeroed()` to the more idiomatic `MaybeUninit` surfaces this false positive and forces an `#[allow]`.

    unsafe { libc::statvfs(path.as_ptr(), &mut s) };
    s.f_blocks as u64

    let mut s = std::mem::MaybeUninit::<libc::statvfs>::uninit();
    unsafe { libc::statvfs(path.as_ptr(), s.as_mut_ptr()) };
    let s = unsafe { s.assume_init() };
    s.f_blocks as u64

body_text:
### What it does

Matching against a single range pattern is equivalent to either an inequality or a `range.contains()` (ie two inequalities) or trivial. This lint would replace `let range = ...` in `if let` statements and let chains.

### Advantage

- Easier to read
- Range pattern matches only work with integers and chars, while inequalities work more generally, so changing the type of the variable being matched would require a smaller change once this lint is applied

### Drawbacks

In const contexts and when the range is either `Range` or `RangeInclusive`, the lint may not be an improvement:
- `Range::contains()` uses `PartialOrd` so cannot be used in const contexts
- `if 3 <= x && x < 5` may be harder to read compared to `if let 3..5 = x` and if `x` is a complex expression then it requires a new binding to maintain the same semantics.

### Example

```rust
if let 2.. = x && let ..10 = y && let 'a'..='z' = c {
    ...
}
```

Could be written as:

```rust
if x >= 2 && y < 10 && ('a'..='z').contains(&c) {
    ...
}
```


### Comparison with existing lints

Instead of being a new lint, this could, or perhaps should, be part of `redundant_pattern_matching`. The lint `equatable_if_let` is also similar.

### Additional Context

### Description

When Clippy looks for its config (starting from `CLIPPY_CONF_DIR`, `CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR` or the current directory and walking up), could it also check `.cargo/clippy.toml` and `.config/clippy.toml` in each directory, after the existing `.clippy.toml` / `clippy.toml`? Existing setups would be unaffected since the current names keep priority.

The motivation is consolidating tool config. Today a typical repo has:

```
.cargo/config.toml     # cargo
.cargo/mutants.toml    # cargo-mutants (default location)
.cargo/deny.toml       # cargo-deny (supported alongside deny.toml)
.config/nextest.toml   # cargo-nextest (only location)
rustfmt.toml           # rustfmt
clippy.toml            # clippy
```

I'm opening similar requests with rustfmt, nextest, cargo-mutants and cargo-deny, asking each to accept `.cargo/<tool>.toml` and `.config/<tool>.toml`.

A workaround exists today, and I've confirmed it works on clippy 0.1.98:

```toml
# .cargo/config.toml
[env]
CLIPPY_CONF_DIR = { value = ".cargo", relative = true }
```

But it's non-obvious, and a project shouldn't need to set an env var just to move a config file.

For reading this config from `Cargo.toml` metadata, there's #10890, which I've also commented on.

### Version

```text
clippy 0.1.98 (48a229ceae 2026-09-01)
```

### Summary

`cast_possible_truncation` knows that `x.min(C)` bounds the value, but only when `C` is a literal. With the same bound written as `u32::MAX as u64`, `u32::MAX.into()` or `u64::from(u32::MAX)` it still fires. The last form is what `cast_lossless` suggests for `u32::MAX as u64`, so following the suggestion of one lint keeps this one firing.

Related: #9613.

### Lint Name

cast_possible_truncation

### Reproducer

I tried this code:

```rust
#![warn(clippy::cast_possible_truncation)]

pub fn literal(x: u64) -> u32 {
    x.min(0xFFFF_FFFF) as u32
}

pub fn cast(x: u64) -> u32 {
    x.min(u32::MAX as u64) as u32
}

pub fn into(x: u64) -> u32 {
    x.min(u32::MAX.into()) as u32
}

pub fn from(x: u64) -> u32 {
    x.min(u64::from(u32::MAX)) as u32
}
```

I saw this happen:

```
warning: casting `u64` to `u32` may truncate the value
 --> lib.rs:8:5
  |
8 |     x.min(u32::MAX as u64) as u32
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  |
  = help: if this is intentional allow the lint with `#[allow(clippy::cast_possible_truncation)]` ...
  = help: for further information visit https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-clippy/rust-1.98.0/index.html#cast_possible_truncation
note: the lint level is defined here
 --> lib.rs:1:9
  |
1 | #![warn(clippy::cast_possible_truncation)]
  |         ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
help: ... or use `try_from` and handle the error accordingly
  |
8 -     x.min(u32::MAX as u64) as u32
8 +     u32::try_from(x.min(u32::MAX as u64))
  |

warning: casting `u64` to `u32` may truncate the value
  --> lib.rs:12:5
   |
12 |     x.min(u32::MAX.into()) as u32
   |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
   |
   = help: if this is intentional allow the lint with `#[allow(clippy::cast_possible_truncation)]` ...
   = help: for further information visit https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-clippy/rust-1.98.0/index.html#cast_possible_truncation
help: ... or use `try_from` and handle the error accordingly
   |
12 -     x.min(u32::MAX.into()) as u32
12 +     u32::try_from(x.min(u32::MAX.into()))
   |

warning: casting `u64` to `u32` may truncate the value
  --> lib.rs:16:5
   |
16 |     x.min(u64::from(u32::MAX)) as u32
   |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
   |
   = help: if this is intentional allow the lint with `#[allow(clippy::cast_possible_truncation)]` ...
   = help: for further information visit https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-clippy/rust-1.98.0/index.html#cast_possible_truncation
help: ... or use `try_from` and handle the error accordingly
   |
16 -     x.min(u64::from(u32::MAX)) as u32
16 +     u32::try_from(x.min(u64::from(u32::MAX)))
   |
```

I expected to see this happen: No warning in any of the four functions, as in `literal`: the value is bounded by `u32::MAX` before the cast.

### Summary

Hi!

Between nightly-2026-08-21 and nightly-2026-08-22, the memory usage of `cargo clippy` has increased a lot. It consumes so much memory that Github Actions kills itself when running `cargo clippy` on our relatively small project (https://github.com/matrix-org/matrix-rust-sdk/).

### Reproducer

```sh
$ # last nightly (2026-09-28)
$ /usr/bin/time -l rustup run nightly cargo clippy --all-targets --features testing -- -D warnings
[snip]
          3980197888  maximum resident set size

$ # nightly 2026-09-07
$ /usr/bin/time -l rustup run nightly-2026-09-07 cargo clippy --all-targets --features testing -- -D warnings
[snip]
          4348116992  maximum resident set size

$ # nightly 2026-08-22
$ /usr/bin/time -l rustup run nightly-2026-08-22 cargo clippy --all-targets --features testing -- -D warnings
[snip]
          3875028992  maximum resident set size

$ # nightly 2026-08-21
$ /usr/bin/time -l rustup run nightly-2026-08-21 cargo clippy --all-targets --features testing -- -D warnings
[snip]
          1875853312  maximum resident set size
```

If I put that in a table, in chronological order, with human numbers:

| nightly date | maximum resident set size |
|-|-|
| 08-21 | 1.87Gb |
| 08-22 | 3.88Gb |
| 09-07 | 4.34Gb |
| 09-28 | 3.98Gb |

### Summary

`significant_drop_tightening` suggests merging the `lock` acquisition into the `HashMap::get`, even though this would cause `data` to be dropped while borrowed. Additionally, the suggested code is missing the `get` call entirely, making it invalid even before the borrow check issue arises.

### Lint Name

significant_drop_tightening

### Reproducer

[Playground link](https://play.rust-lang.org/?version=stable&mode=debug&edition=2024&gist=86fc7c6dea9a4e9b5ffdffaf2bfac049)

I tried this code:

```rust
#![deny(clippy::significant_drop_tightening)]

use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::sync::Mutex;

fn main() {
    let map = Mutex::new(HashMap::from([(String::from("test"), String::new())]));
    let key = String::from("test");
    let lock = map.lock().unwrap();
    let data = lock.get(&key).expect("key should exist");
    println!("{data}")
}
```

I saw this happen:

```
    Checking playground v0.0.1 (/playground)
error: temporary with significant `Drop` can be early dropped
  --> src/main.rs:9:9
   |
 6 |   fn main() {
   |  ___________-
 7 | |     let map = Mutex::new(HashMap::from([(String::from("test"), String::new())]));
 8 | |     let key = String::from("test");
 9 | |     let lock = map.lock().unwrap();
   | |         ^^^^
10 | |     let data = lock.get(&key).expect("key should exist");
11 | |     println!("{data}")
12 | | }
   | |_- temporary `lock` is currently being dropped at the end of its contained scope

note: the lint level is defined here
  --> src/main.rs:1:9
   |
 1 | #![deny(clippy::significant_drop_tightening)]
   |         ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
help: merge the temporary construction with its single usage

body_text:
### Summary

`transmute_undefined_repr` doesn't fire on a transmute between a type and a single-field struct that has the default representation. A common case is `&str` to `&Wrapper` where `struct Wrapper(str)`.

The layout of a `repr(Rust)` struct isn't guaranteed, even when it has only one field. The [Reference](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/type-layout.html#the-default-representation) says the default representation gives no guarantees about data layout. The [Nomicon](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nomicon/transmutes.html) says only `#[repr(C)]` or `#[repr(transparent)]` give a layout you can rely on. So this transmute relies on how the compiler currently lays the type out, which is what this lint is meant to catch.

The cause is `reduce_ty`: a struct whose only non-zero-sized field is `T` reduces to `T` before the `repr` is checked. `def.repr().inhibit_struct_field_reordering()` is only checked for structs with more than one non-zero-sized field. Because of this, `&str -> &Wrapper` is analysed as `&str -> &str`.

This seems to be deliberate. #8503 described one-field structs as intentionally not linted, and #8547 made one-element tuples behave the same way. I'd like to suggest changing that: only treat a single-field struct as its field when it is `#[repr(transparent)]`, or `#[repr(C)]` with that field first. In every other case, report an undefined layout as the lint does today. The lint is in nursery, so this seems like the right place to be strict, but I understand it may create a lot of new warnings in existing code (see #8496).

This came up in a real crate. A `#[repr(transparent)]` was missing on one of many otherwise identical wrapper types whose `from_borrowed_unchecked` transmutes `&str -> &Self` (ruma/ruma#2625). Nothing in clippy pointed it out.

### Lint Name

transmute_undefined_repr

### Reproducer

I tried this code:

```rust
pub struct Name(str);

pub fn from_str(s: &str) -> &Name {
    unsafe { std::mem::transmute::<&str, &Name>(s) }
}
```

with `cargo clippy -- -D clippy::transmute_undefined_repr`.

I expected to see this happen: an error saying that `&Name` has an undefined layout, with a suggestion to add `#[repr(transparent)]` to `Name`.

Instead, this happened: no error from `transmute_undefined_repr`. The only warning was the unrelated `dead_code` warning for the unread field.

The same thing happens with sized fields: `pub struct Meters(pub f64)` with `transmute::<&f64, &Meters>` doesn't trigger the lint either.

### Version

```text
rustc 1.99.0 (b940084d7 2026-09-28)

commit-hash: b940084d7eb6a299eb4bfeb8e34901bc051e7ac4
commit-date: 2026-09-28
host: aarch64-apple-darwin
release: 1.99.0
LLVM version: 23.1.1

{"repository": "rust-lang/rust-clippy", "task_candidate_id": 23668, "repository_id": 258, "issue_number": 17869, "github_issue_id": 5824122384, "html_url": "https://github.com/rust-lang/rust-clippy/issues/17869", "created_at": "2026-10-13T03:42:58+00:00", "author_association": "NONE", "title": "transmute_undefined_repr: no lint when transmuting into a single-field struct without `#[repr(transparent)]`", "body_text": "### Summary

`transmute_undefined_repr` doesn't fire on a transmute between a type and a single-field struct that has the default representation. A common case is `&str` to `&Wrapper` where `struct Wrapper(str)`.

The layout of a `repr(Rust)` struct isn't guaranteed, even when it has only one field. The [Reference](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/type-layout.html#the-default-representation) says the default representation gives no guarantees about data layout. The [Nomicon](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nomicon/transmutes.html) says only `#[repr(C)]` or `#[repr(transparent)]` give a layout you can rely on. So this transmute relies on how the compiler currently lays the type out, which is what this lint is meant to catch.

The cause is `reduce_ty`: a struct whose only non-zero-sized field is `T` reduces to `T` before the `repr` is checked. `def.repr().inhibit_struct_field_reordering()` is only checked for structs with more than one non-zero-sized field. Because of this, `&str -> &Wrapper` is analysed as `&str -> &str`.

This seems to be deliberate. #8503 described one-field structs as intentionally not linted, and #8547 made one-element tuples behave the same way. I'd like to suggest changing that: only treat a single-field struct as its field when it is `#[repr(transparent)]`, or `#[repr(C)]` with that field first. In every other case, report an undefined layout as the lint does today. The lint is in nursery, so this seems like the right place to be strict, but I understand it may create a lot of new warnings in existing code (see #8496).

This came up in a real crate. A `#[repr(transparent)]` was missing on one of many otherwise identical wrapper types whose `from_borrowed_unchecked` transmutes `&str -> &Self` (ruma/ruma#2625). Nothing in clippy pointed it out.

### Lint Name

transmute_undefined_repr

### Reproducer

I tried this code:

```rust
pub struct Name(str);

pub fn from_str(s: &str) -> &Name {
    unsafe { std::mem::transmute::<&str, &Name>(s) }
}
```

with `cargo clippy -- -D clippy::transmute_undefined_repr`.

I expected to see this happen: an error saying that `&Name` has an undefined layout, with a suggestion to add `#[repr(transparent)]` to `Name`.

Instead, this happened: no error from `transmute_undefined_repr`. The only warning was the unrelated `dead_code` warning for the unread field.

The same thing happens with sized fields: `pub struct Meters(pub f64)` with `transmute::<&f64, &Meters>` doesn't trigger the lint either.

### Summary

If I set `rust-version = "1.85"`, I don't see a `clippy::incompatible_msrv` when I use the `std::assert_matches!` macro.


### Lint Name

incompatible_msrv

### Reproducer

I tried this code ([playground](https://play.rust-lang.org/?version=nightly&mode=debug&edition=2024&gist=183304b881ef35c0eabd482e1560b637)):

```rust
#![warn(clippy::incompatible_msrv)]

#[clippy::msrv = "1.85"]
fn main() {
  let x = Some(7u32);
  std::assert_matches!(x, Some(y) if y > 3);
  // this does get a warning
  let z = 3u32.strict_add(5);
}
```

I expected to see this happen:
An `clippy::incompatible_msrv` lint saying `std::assert_matches` can't be used until Rust 1.96.

Instead, I saw no warnings.

### Related Comment?

https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/19833af7224424e8b53e288097d56b6af43d5bcf/src/tools/clippy/clippy_lints/src/incompatible_msrv.rs#L183-L194

### Version

body_text:
The default crypto provider for Rustls (starting from version 0.23) is aws-lc-rs and it make sense. 

However for windows platforms, symcrypt should be used as the default crypto provider. This choice aligns with Windows-native cryptographic primitives and leverages deep Azure and Microsoft ecosystem integration. Using symcrypt also enables reuse of the existing internal crypto stack, reduces duplication, and ensures better compatibility with platform security features, updates, and validation processes.

I understand that it can be selected through features, but I guess default selection should be one best for platform and then if someone wants can choose not to use default based on scenario specific requirement.

Hi all!

We discovered when attempting to bump rustls in https://github.com/DataDog/saluki to resolve RUSTSEC-2026-0285 that rustls [was updated to use aws-lc-rs 1.18](https://github.com/rustls/rustls/pull/3203). aws-lc-rs 1.18 depends on a version of the FIPS module (aws-lc 4.x) that isn't yet FIPS certified and so we'd like to stick with aws-lc-rs 1.17 (which depends on the certified 3.x) until it is.

**Checklist**
* [x] I've searched the issue tracker for similar requests
* [x] I've confirmed my request is for a semver-incompatible update

**Is your dependency update request related to a problem? Please describe.**

Blocked from upgrading rustls to latest due to dependency on an uncertificed aws-lc-rs version.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

Would you be open to either:
- Maintaining a version of rustls with security updates that depends on aws-ls-rs 1.17 (AWS itself seems to be maintaining the 1.17 version in addition to 1.18 while FIPS certification proceeds)
- Simply downgrading rustls to depend on aws-rc-ls 1.17 for now

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

Simply ignoring the vulnerability in rustls.  This is what we've done temporarily: https://github.com/DataDog/saluki/pull/2606

body_text:
**Checklist**
* [x] I've searched the issue tracker for similar bugs.

**Describe the bug**

This is a follow-up to #3301 / #3332, asking about the 0.23.x line.

On `main`, #3332 makes a buffered write that hits the TLS 1.2 confidentiality limit return `Err(Error::EncryptError)`, and later writes fail too. The 0.23.46 backport (ab3ca337cc, 9363630547) stops partial writes and stops encrypting with the exhausted key, but `Writer::write` still returns `Ok(len)` for data that is never encrypted or sent:

- `CommonState::send_appdata_encrypt` does `return len;` when `check_pre_encrypt_action(last)` fails.
- `send_close_notify()` does not set `core.state`, so `check_error()` lets later writes through. Each one logs `traffic keys exhausted` again and also returns `Ok(len)`.
- The rel-0.23 tests treat this as expected: `tls12_connection_fails_after_alert_at_confidentiality_limit` does `client.writer().write_all(b"later").unwrap()`.

The caller cannot tell the bytes were dropped. It also cannot tell the connection is now write-dead, until the peer closes it.

**Real-world impact**

This shows up in GreptimeDB's Kafka remote WAL (GreptimeTeam/greptimedb#9681), using rskafka + tokio-rustls over TLS 1.2 to AWS MSK. MSK offers neither TLS 1.3 nor ChaCha20-Poly1305, so AES-GCM and its 2^24-record limit are unavoidable there.

1. The client hits the limit. rustls queues `close_notify`, and every request written after that "succeeds" (`Ok(len)`) without being sent.
2. The Kafka broker defers closing when `close_notify` arrives in the same read as preceding application data (a separate Kafka issue). Because the client sends nothing more, the broker never closes the socket.
3. rskafka waits for responses that will never come, so every in-flight request hangs until the request timeout instead of failing fast and reconnecting.

If the write returned an error, rskafka would poison the connection right away and retry on a new one.

**To Reproduce**

The existing rel-0.23 tests show it: in `tls12_connection_fails_after_alert_at_confidentiality_limit`, the `write_all(b"later")` after exhaustion returns `Ok`. #9681 has an end-to-end repro with Kafka 3.9 limited to TLSv1.2 and a lowered `confidentiality_limit`.

**Applicable Version(s)**

rustls 0.23.46 (also 0.23.45 and earlier), tokio-rustls 0.26, Linux x86_64.

**Expected behavior**

Same as `main` after #3332: the write that cannot be encrypted, and every later write, returns an error. For example, an `io::Error` wrapping `Error::EncryptError`, like `check_error()` already does for other fatal errors.

**Questions**

1. Was keeping `Ok(..)` in 0.23 a deliberate compatibility decision, or would a backport of the error-returning behavior to `rel-0.23` be accepted?
2. If a backport is welcome, which do you prefer: storing the error in `core.state` (simplest, but it also fails the read side), or a write-only flag so already-received responses stay readable after `close_notify`?

I'm happy to send a PR against `rel-0.23` once the direction is clear.

Note for async users: the fix needs to be an `Err`, not `Ok(0)`. tokio-rustls's `poll_write` would spin on `Ok(0)` when `wants_write()` is false.

* [x] I've searched the issue tracker for similar bugs.

**Describe the bug**

This is a follow-up to #3301 / #3332, asking about the 0.23.x line.

On `main`, #3332 makes a buffered write that hits the TLS 1.2 confidentiality limit return `Err(Error::EncryptError)`, and later writes fail too. The 0.23.46 backport (ab3ca337cc, 9363630547) stops partial writes and stops encrypting with the exhausted key, but `Writer::write` still returns `Ok(len)` for data that is never encrypted or sent:

- `CommonState::send_appdata_encrypt` does `return len;` when `check_pre_encrypt_action(last)` fails.
- `send_close_notify()` does not set `core.state`, so `check_error()` lets later writes through. Each one logs `traffic keys exhausted` again and also returns `Ok(len)`.
- The rel-0.23 tests treat this as expected: `tls12_connection_fails_after_alert_at_confidentiality_limit` does `client.writer().write_all(b"later").unwrap()`.

The caller cannot tell the bytes were dropped. It also cannot tell the connection is now write-dead, until the peer closes it.

**Real-world impact**

This shows up in GreptimeDB's Kafka remote WAL (GreptimeTeam/greptimedb#9681), using rskafka + tokio-rustls over TLS 1.2 to AWS MSK. MSK offers neither TLS 1.3 nor ChaCha20-Poly1305, so AES-GCM and its 2^24-record limit are unavoidable there.

1. The client hits the limit. rustls queues `close_notify`, and every request written after that "succeeds" (`Ok(len)`) without being sent.
2. The Kafka broker defers closing when `close_notify` arrives in the same read as preceding application data (a separate Kafka issue). Because the client sends nothing more, the broker never closes the socket.
3. rskafka waits for responses that will never come, so every in-flight request hangs until the request timeout instead of failing fast and reconnecting.

If the write returned an error, rskafka would poison the connection right away and retry on a new one.

**To Reproduce**

The existing rel-0.23 tests show it: in `tls12_connection_fails_after_alert_at_confidentiality_limit`, the `write_all(b"later")` after exhaustion returns `Ok`. #9681 has an end-to-end repro with Kafka 3.9 limited to TLSv1.2 and a lowered `confidentiality_limit`.

**Applicable Version(s)**

rustls 0.23.46 (also 0.23.45 and earlier), tokio-rustls 0.26, Linux x86_64.

**Expected behavior**

Same as `main` after #3332: the write that cannot be encrypted, and every later write, returns an error. For example, an `io::Error` wrapping `Error::EncryptError`, like `check_error()` already does for other fatal errors.

**Questions**

1. Was keeping `Ok(..)` in 0.23 a deliberate compatibility decision, or would a backport of the error-returning behavior to `rel-0.23` be accepted?
2. If a backport is welcome, which do you prefer: storing the error in `core.state` (simplest, but it also fails the read side), or a write-only flag so already-received responses stay readable after `close_notify`?

I'm happy to send a PR against `rel-0.23` once the direction is clear.

Note for async users: the fix needs to be an `Err`, not `Ok(0)`. tokio-rustls's `poll_write` would spin on `Ok(0)` when `wants_write()` is false.

This crate supports `no_std` conditionally:
https://github.com/rustls/rustls/blob/56a02126e79afe260ffbdf306c44c9641437a5ed/rustls-aws-lc-rs/src/lib.rs#L24

But one of its dependencies (`aws-lc-rs`, version `1.18.1`) does not support `no_std` and pulls in `std` transitively:
https://github.com/rustls/rustls/blob/56a02126e79afe260ffbdf306c44c9641437a5ed/rustls-aws-lc-rs/Cargo.toml#L19

As a result, builds targeting bare-metal or other `no_std`-only targets fail to compile, even though the crate itself contains no direct `std` usage.

While working on improving the documentation for the pyramid functions
(#8029), I noticed that several other functions in `skimage.transform`
(such as `resize`, `warp`, and some related helpers) also accept a `mode`
parameter.

These functions follow the `numpy.pad` convention for `mode` values, and
internally map them to the corresponding `scipy.ndimage` boundary modes.
However, this mapping is not always clearly documented in the associated
docstrings.

Because of this, users switching between NumPy/SciPy and scikit-image APIs
may find the behavior confusing or inconsistent.

It might be useful to clarify this more explicitly across
`skimage.transform`, either by adding a short note to the relevant
docstrings or by referencing a shared explanation.

If this sounds reasonable to the maintainers, I’d be happy to follow up
with a PR.

We have two requirements:

- (a) When a user imports `skimage2`, they should see a `ExperimentalAPIWarning`
- (b) We want to import `skimage2` ourselves internally in `skiamge` in wrappers around ported functions without triggering that warning.

I've been thinking how to satisfy both requirements because our current setup violates (b). I haven't yet found a good way to address this yet.

I thought that adding something like 
```python
# skimage/_shared/__init__.py
import warnings

with warnings.catch_warnings():
    warnings.filterwarnings(
        action="ignore",
        message="Importing from the `skimage2` namespace is experimental.",
        category=UserWarning,
    )

### Description:

I was experimenting with `slic` and ran it on a 3D (60, 256, 256) image, and was surprised to see a 2D return array.   This is because the routine assumed (`channel_axis=-1`) that the last axis was a color axis.   Obviously, in this case that doesn't make sense, because, as far as I can see, a channel axis has to be length 3 or length 4.   Is that assumption correct?   And if so, would it be worth adding a check that the length is `in (3, 4)` and raising an error otherwise, on the basis the user has likely made a mistake?

body_text:
In `tests/skimage/metrics/test_structural_similarity.py`, `test_structural_similarity_nD` constructs test arrays using `* 5` instead of `* ndim`:

```python
for ndim in range(1, 5):
    xsize = [N] * 5  # should this be `* ndim`?
    X = (rng.rand(*xsize) * 255).astype(dtype)
    Y = (rng.rand(*xsize) * 255).astype(dtype)
```

`ndim` is effectively unused — arrays are always 5-dimensional regardless of the loop variable.

Changing `* 5` → `* ndim` causes failures:
```
FAILED test_structural_similarity_nD[uint8] - assert np.float64(0.12033917126639686) < 0.05
FAILED test_structural_similarity_nD[float32] - assert np.float64(0.12066029480774887) < 0.05
FAILED test_structural_similarity_nD[float64] - assert np.float64(0.12066033348447812) < 0.05
```

Questions:
- Was `* 5` intentional? If so, what does the `ndim` loop actually exercise?
- If it should be `* ndim`, the `< 0.05` threshold likely needs revisiting for lower-dimensional inputs.

Noted in PR #8084.

body_text:
### Description:

The `benchmarks/` suite reinstated in #8273 imports exclusively from `skimage` (v1). skimage v1 is slated for removal, and several of its functions already just re-export `_skimage2` implementations directly (for example, `src/skimage/filters/_gaussian.py` imports `difference_of_gaussians` straight from `_skimage2.filters._gaussian`). Once v1 is removed, the benchmark suite will fail outright, since nothing it imports will exist anymore.

Benchmarks should target `skimage2` (or `_skimage2`) directly so they keep working after v1's removal and measure the code that actually ships.

This isn't urgent. `skimage2`'s API is still experimental and its migration from v1 is partial, so retargeting the suite today would mean measuring a mix of migrated and not-yet-migrated functions against a moving target. Better to wait until `skimage2`'s API is closer to stable, or track migration progress per module and update the corresponding benchmark file as each area lands.

body_text:
### Description:

A local `spin asv -- continuous main` measures something different from what the pull request check measures, in three ways:

- It runs the benchmarks marked slow, which the pull request check skips.
- It judges results against `asv`'s default comparison factor, which is tighter than the one CI uses to absorb the noise of a shared runner. A local result and a CI result can disagree on the same change.
- It runs the whole suite, rather than narrowing to the benchmarks covering the subpackages the branch touches.

The environment variables controlling the first two aren't documented, so reproducing a CI result locally means reading the workflow.

`spin asv` should be able to measure what a CI run measures, and to scope itself to the subpackages you've changed. The settings behind that should be defined once and read by both CI and the local tooling, rather than written separately in each, since values duplicated across the two drift apart.

This was built and reviewed as part of #8273, then split back out to keep that pull request reviewable. An implementation plan, with the commits to recover it from and the constraints that only surfaced by running it, is at https://gist.github.com/blink1073/4184a272852bdc6b8ff47b438bf64808

### What's happening

`blob_dog` crashes with an `OverflowError` instead of a clear error
message when `min_sigma=0` is passed. This should either work, or fail
with a helpful validation message — right now it fails in a confusing way.

### How to reproduce it

```python
import numpy as np
from skimage.feature import blob_dog

image = np.zeros((10, 10))
blob_dog(image, min_sigma=0)
```

### What actually happens




### Why it fails

- Inside `blob_dog`, the number of scale-space steps is calculated as:
  `k = int(np.mean(np.log(max_sigma / min_sigma) / np.log(sigma_ratio) + 1))`
- When `min_sigma` is `0`, `max_sigma / min_sigma` divides by zero and
  becomes `inf`
- `np.log(inf)` is still `inf`
- Python can't convert `inf` into an integer, so `int(inf)` throws
  `OverflowError`
- There's no check anywhere in the function that stops `min_sigma=0`
  from reaching this line in the first place

### Evidence this is a real, reproducible bug

- **Reproduced in two separate environments**: a local development build,
  and a fresh Google Colab session using the officially released
  `pip install scikit-image` package — same crash, same traceback, in both
- **Not an isolated fluke**: this same failure pattern (a silent
  divide-by-zero followed by `OverflowError: cannot convert float
  infinity to integer`) has appeared before in this codebase, in a
  different function — see #5252 (`skimage.transform.rescale` with
  `scale < 0.2`)
- **Existing precedent for the fix**: `blob_dog` already validates one of
  its other parameters (`sigma_ratio <= 1.0`) with a clear `ValueError`
  near the top of the function — so adding a similar check for
  `min_sigma` follows a pattern the maintainers already use in this exact
  file
- **Confirmed no existing test covers this**: none of the existing tests
  for `blob_dog` use `min_sigma=0` or any value near it, and the
  function's docstring doesn't mention that `0` is invalid

### Suggested fix

Add a validation check near the top of `blob_dog` (and likely `blob_log`,
which uses the same pattern) that raises a clear error, for example:

```python
if np.any(np.asarray(min_sigma) <= 0):
    raise ValueError("min_sigma must be > 0")
```

### Description:

SPEC 0 recommends dropping Python 3.12 and several core dependency versions in [2026 Q4](https://scientific-python.org/specs/spec-0000/#2026---quarter-4). This issue tracks that bump for scikit-image and the code cleanups it unlocks.

**Raise Python floor to 3.13**

- [ ] `pyproject.toml`: `requires-python = '>=3.13'`
- [ ] Remove the `Programming Language :: Python :: 3.12` classifier
- [ ] Drop 3.12 from CI matrices and `spin` / tooling config

**Dependency floors (SPEC 0 2026 Q4)**

| Package | Current | New | SPEC 0 drop |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| numpy | `>=2.1` | `>=2.3` | 2.2.0 (Dec 2024) |
| networkx | `>=3.0` | `>=3.5` | 3.4 (Oct 2024) |
| scikit-learn | `>=1.6` | `>=1.7` | 1.6.0 (Dec 2024) |
| scipy (emscripten) | `>=1.14` | `>=1.15` | align with the non-emscripten pin |

- [ ] Update the pins in `pyproject.toml` and regenerate `requirements/*.txt` with `tools/generate_requirements.py`
- [ ] With `numpy>=2.3`, remove any `np.__version__` guards for pre-2.3 behavior

**Code cleanups unlocked by the 3.13 floor**

- [ ] `src/_skimage2/_shared/utils.py` (~L722): drop the `sys.version_info[:2] < (3, 13)` branch; keep the un-indented `.. deprecated::` note
- [ ] `src/_skimage2/measure/_regionprops.py` (~L1481): keep only the `>= (3, 13)` doc-parse regex; drop the fallback
- [ ] `tests/skimage2/_shared/test_utils.py` (~L227): inline the `inspect.cleandoc`-adjusted expected docstring; drop the version check
- [ ] `src/_skimage2/_shared/utils.py` (~L794): remove the `sys.version < '3'` Python 2 branch

**Follow-up: adopt new stdlib**

- [ ] Replace the function-level path in `deprecate_func` (`src/_skimage2/_shared/utils.py`) with the stdlib `warnings.deprecated` decorator ([PEP 702](https://peps.python.org/pep-0702/)).  Example:

```python
from warnings import deprecated

### Description:

Discussing the coordinate refactoring with Claude, the following problem came up.  I wrote all this myself.

How should `rotate` (and `swirl`) behave in `skimage2` conventions?

In `skimage2`, `warp` will consider input coordinates to be row, col (i, j) rather than col, row order.   The upshot is that, in `skimage2` - `warp(img, SimilarityTransform(rotation=0.2))` will have the visual effect of rotating the image *clockwise* around its 0, 0 pixel, whereas in `skimage2` the same code will rotate the image *anti-clockwise*.

However, what should `rotate(img, 0.2)` do?   At the moment, this rotates the image counter-clockwise around the center of the image.    This behavior then differs from the `warp` case. 

However, we never stated that `warp(img, SimilarityTransform(rotation=0.2))` should be interpreted in the same way as `rotate(img, 0.2)` (modulo the center of rotation).   So one could argue that it would be reasonable to leave `rotate` (and similarly `swirl`) as specifically *visual* rotations, and therefore leave their behavior unchanged.   I personally think it would be cleaner to make rotation mean the same thing in either case, so make `rotate` (`swirl`) reverse direction in `skimage2`.

What do y'all think?

### Description:

It turns out that trying to fix an apparently simple problem in `hessian_matrix` (the `order='xy'` equivalent for `skimage2`) has led to the escape of some rather frightening and large insects.

Among these is that the `hessian` filter appears to be badly broken - and has been since it reached the code-base.  Exploration here:

https://scikit-image.org/skimage-workbooks/on-hessian-filter/

Our options are:

* To remove it entirely in `skimage2` and wait for someone to ask for it, or
* To write it correctly from the paper, probably renamed as `hessian_hybrid`.

The second isn't too hard (see the notebook), but - is it worth it?

### Description:

`skimage.transform.radon` fails for valid 2-D images with a singleton height when `circle=True` (the default).

Although a `(5, 1)` image is handled and produces `(1, 180)`, a `(1, 5)` image raises a `ValueError`, and a `(1, 1)` image raises an `IndexError`. I expect all of these cases to return `(1, 180)`, with `radon(image)` producing the same result as `radon(image.T)` for these cases.

The problem appears to stem from constructing the `ogrid` coordinate arrays with `np.array(..., dtype=object)`, which behaves incorrectly for singleton dimensions.

### Way to reproduce:

```python
import numpy as np
from skimage.transform import radon

for shape in [(5, 1), (1, 5), (1, 1)]:
    try:
        print(shape, radon(np.ones(shape), circle=True).shape)
    except Exception as e:
        print(shape, type(e).__name__, e)
```

**Output**
```text
(5, 1) (1, 180)
(1, 5) ValueError: could not broadcast input array from shape (5,) into shape (1,)
(1, 1) IndexError: boolean index did not match indexed array along axis 1; size of axis is 1 but size of corresponding boolean axis is 2
```

### Version information:

```Shell
3.12.3 (main, Aug 31 2026, 10:18:26) [GCC 13.3.0]
Linux-6.6.87.2-microsoft-standard-WSL2-x86_64-with-glibc2.39

numpy version: 2.5.3
```

### Description:

Recently NumPy implemented `minmax`: https://github.com/numpy/numpy/pull/32231

[The `minmax` function]( https://numpy.org/devdocs/reference/generated/numpy.minmax.html ) provides a fast path in cases where both `min` and `max` of an array are needed. `minmax` will be [included in NumPy 2.6.0]( https://numpy.org/devdocs/release/2.6.0-notes.html#new-function-numpy-minmax ).

Code paths in scikit-image that make use of both `min` and `max` may benefit from `minmax` when available.

For example `rescale_minmax` could use `minmax` here:

https://github.com/scikit-image/scikit-image/blob/b700edc8005e4ee9e74fc83259f09e8df3213f15/src/_skimage2/util/_value_rescaling.py#L50-L51

Some metric functions upcast to max float type (via `_max_precision_float_dtype`) during computation; for example `confusion_matrix_at_thresholds` does this because it uses `cumulative_sum`, which suffers from precision degradation due to error accumulation. (Aside, note that we return arrays at max dtype, and do not convert back to input dtype).

Some estimators also upcast during computation, e.g., `RidgeCV`, but we return attribute arrays to input array dtype (AFAICT) so the 'output' dtype is matches input dtype.

If the user is using a device that only supports float 32 (i.e. MPS), it is possible that they suffer from precision problems when using these metrics/estimators. Currently, we inform users of this by adding a "(see [Note on device support for float64](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/modules/array_api.html#device-support-for-float64))" beside that estimator/metric in our docs.

This also affects the mixed array namespace/device inputs situation (wrt metric functions see #31274 and #32755 and wrt fit and predict see #33076). If we are moving arrays to a device where only float32 is supported, precision may be affected for the above estimators/metrics.

How do we remember to document this and make it clear to people reading the code that a downcast is occurring? Options discussed during the last array API meeting (not mutually exclusive):

* Use existing estimator tag system to tag estimators affected
   * this excludes metrics. Note that although we do check that the output of metrics with different array namespace inputs matches that of numpy, this will not always pick up on precision problems as it is data dependent 
* Add a `dtype` kwarg to `move_to` - this would make it clearer in the code that a potential downcast was occurring (see discussion https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/32755#discussion_r2611300838)
   * though this would make it more difficult to use the same `move_to` function for both array conversion and 'converting' an estimator, see: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/33076#discussion_r2822481554

In #16723 and #17026 we deployed airspeed velocity (asv) benchmarks. For a while now, they are offline. This is unfortunate because:
- It is harder to detect regressions.
- We don’t see the big time improvements in the last releases.

This issue is to track the (re-) deployment of the ASV benchmarks until they are back online.

body_text:
Now that we have added array API support to several important models and tools (including classifiers, regressors, transformers, meta estimators, pipelines, evaluation and model selection tools...), it might be important to discuss what are our plans and conditions to remove the "experimental" marker for that set of features.

To me, moving out of experimental means the following things in particular:

- a. Setting `array_api_dispatch=True` as the default value in the config (or maybe even deprecate this configuration parameter to always have it enabled and simplify the code as a result);
- b. Enforcing backward compatibility guarantees with array API related behavior change (the requirement for 2 release deprecation cycle and the introduction of `FutureWarning`).

For a., I think we would need to:

- [ ] ensure that all estimators and public functions/classes that have not yet been updated to support array API inputs do not raise confusing error messages on non-(NumPy + CPU) inputs when array API dispatch is enabled. I have no idea if this is the case or not. We should probably extend the common test to check that.

Furthermore, for a. to make sense we might need to wait for SciPy to also enable array API support without having the user to manually set `SCIPY_ARRAY_API=1`, and therefore:

- [x] coordinate with upstream on their own plans to move out of experimental.
  - SciPy has an open discussion about this here: https://discuss.scientific-python.org/t/making-array-types-support-public-scipy-2-0/2355 

I think that for point b. we at least need to implement the following:

- [x] finalize https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/32755 to ensure consistency in mixed namespace inputs for metric functions;
- [x] at least the common testing infrastructure for https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/28668 (to make sure that we agree on the semantics) and possibly also upgrade all our existing estimators to ensure that they pass this new common test.
- [x] https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/33076
- [x] https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/34824

- [ ] at least one runnable example in our doc that shows how to use scikit-learn estimators in a non-trivial pipeline with on a non-CPU device (when available).

Then we need to make sure we can run the full test suite with array API dispatch enabled. This would entails either:

- [ ] https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/34324 (but this sounds complex and ugly to maintain)

or alternatively, we could agree on:

- [ ] https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/34604

Just before moving out of experimental:

- [ ] https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/34135

The purpose of this issue is to agree with a shared plan and maybe milestone this as a goal for 1.9?
