### Describe the workflow you want to enable

When fitting a `NuSVC` it might happen than the regularisation parameter `nu` is unfeasible with respect to the class (un)balancing.

Currently `_base.py` features the evaluation of the kernel function (if callable), that is:
```python
        if callable(self.kernel):
            # you must store a reference to X to compute the kernel in predict
            # TODO: add keyword copy to copy on demand
            self.__Xfit = X
            X = self._compute_kernel(X)

            if X.shape[0] != X.shape[1]:
                raise ValueError("X.shape[0] should be equal to X.shape[1]")
```
and this operation is done _before_ calling `libsvm.fit()`, which internally checks for nu feasibility.

This means that if a kernel is expensive to evaluate (say, string kernels or graph kernels), the end user must wait for quite a long time before eventually hitting the infamous "specified nu is unfeasible" error message.

### Describe your proposed solution

Do a check on `nu` feasibility before calculating the kernel matrix in case the kernel is a callable. Is this manner the user knows straight away that `nu` has to be lowered rather than waiting for a (potentially heavy) kernel matrix evaluation, whose shape or values have no role on the feasibility of `nu`.

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

### Describe the workflow you want to enable

The `Ridge` family is already compatible with the Array API, which is great for pytorch compatibility! It simplifies linear probing evaluations for foundation models. 

However, these models often use datasets with many examples.
It is not always feasible to accumulate features in memory before passing them to a ridge classifier.

It would be nice if `Ridge` had a `partial_fit` method which allowed processing the dataset in batches. 
With $D$ features and $N$ examples, `Ridge` would only accumulate the features statistics ($D \times D$) instead of all the features ($N \times D$)

### Describe your proposed solution

We accumulate the sufficient statistics $A = X^\top X \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times D}$ and $B = X^\top Y \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times C}$, both of size independent of $N$. The closed-form ridge solution is $W = (A + \lambda I)^{-1} B$. Because $X$ is never materialized, memory is $O(D^2)$ instead of $O(ND)$, so the probe scales to arbitrarily large train sets.


### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

Implement it outside of scikit learn: https://github.com/braindecode/OpenEEGBench/blob/ede655f1294feef15ff6be4d6e6d94628ab9187e/open_eeg_bench/ridge_probe.py#L79-L273
Then add a test for consistency with the scikit learn pipeline on a small random datasets: https://github.com/braindecode/OpenEEGBench/blob/ede655f1294feef15ff6be4d6e6d94628ab9187e/tests/test_ridge_probe.py#L42-L99

### Additional context

We are using this for [OpenEEGBench](https://github.com/braindecode/OpenEEGBench), a library for benchmarking EEG foundation models. 

Context: https://github.com/braindecode/OpenEEGBench/pull/32#discussion_r3172514283

> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Describe the workflow you want to enable

From: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/33354#issue-3973551384, we want to enable:

1. [ ] [Optimization] Add a bitset cache (i.e. a uint64_t memory view) that allows us to compute the category split as we traverse the tree for inference speedup
2. [ ] [Feature] Support in tree-based ensemble models (RF + ExtraTrees). This could be done after for random splitter support, so we do all the classes at once: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/34832/
4. [x] [Refactor] Consolidate the goes_left operation to work at inference time too: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/33972
5. [x] [Refactor] Understand the bitset operations and merge these with the HistGradientBoosting bitset operations https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/33354)
6. [x] [Feature] Implement categorical splitting for RandomSplitter for ExtraTrees. Pretty easy now that we have an arbitrary sized bitset, which we can expand to hold many categories in the case of a randomized tree: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/33972
8. [ ] [Feature] Add support for categorical in exporting 
9. [x] [Feature] Add internal ordinal encoding support for any kind of "categorical input" (see https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/33354#discussion_r3199995969)
10. [ ] [Refactor] Address refactoring to use ColumnTransformer in tree, similar to HGBT: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/33354#discussion_r3521665892
11. [ ] Add warm_start capability with categorical_features (see: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/34832#discussion_r4003388745_)

Below the line for priority:
1. [ ] [Feature] Brute-force search; expands categorical support to multi-class and multi-output problems
2. [ ] [Feature] Add support for sparse categorical splitting with best and random splitter

### Describe your proposed solution

These work streams may not all be relevant, or mergable, but we can explore.

> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

_Maintainer note: I am planning out my own work here. If you're not in the scikit-learn organisation, please refrain from opening a PR._

There are several steps to take to de-tangle the design of the metadata routing module in `sklearn/utils/_metadata_requests.py` and the utilities and tests around that module. The current design often intertwines several functionalities, so it will take several iterations to take them apart. The goal is to make metadata routing simpler and easier to maintain by the 1.10 release in November 2026.

I would like to lead a series of PRs that result in a simpler design. Each PR should leave metadata routing in a working, tested state; the full simplification is visible only across the series.

This issue tracks the planned steps. I will update and adjust as I go.

## Goal

Simpler, easier-to-maintain metadata routing by **1.10** (Nov 2026), or anytime in the future.

## Possible measures (to check for feasibility)

- [ ] **#34314**  (`__sklearn_get_metadata_request__`, docs, tests) (new feature, rather than simplification but unblocks #31695)
- [ ] use new developer API in _BaseScorer: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/34314#discussion_r3473901297
- [ ] **#31695**
- [ ] **Split `_get_metadata_request`** into two functions; clone stored `_metadata_request` vs build defaults (see [#34314 comment](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/34314#issuecomment-4777556515))
- [ ] **Split `__sklearn_get_metadata_request__`** into two functions (see https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/34314#issuecomment-4777556515)
- [ ] **Naming cleanup**: align parameter names (`method`, `kwargs`, `props`, `parent`, …) across the module
- [ ] clean up what "default requests" means in the variable names and internal docs (this term currently can mean many different things)
- [ ] define what metadata is within scikit-learn positively (list of things metadata can be), instead of negatively (collecting all from the signatures and excluding some by filtering, UNUSED flag, ...)
- [ ] [remove the  "always ignore the first param" rule](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/34314#discussion_r3684322308)
- [ ] With auto-requests to come, we deal with a complicated 4-step mechanism to set routing requests in consumers:
    1. signature-sniffing for setting requests to `None`
    2. overriding with class-level `__metadata_request__*`, 
    3. overrriding with auto-requests in runtime (but only allowing for `True` values), 
    4. overriding with user-set requests 
  We should check what we can do to simplify that.
- [ ] Check if we can get rid of the distinction between `SIMPLE_METHODS` and `COMPOSITE_METHODS` and threat them equally, see https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/31413/changes#r3853537529. We did this in several past PRs already, but for a larger scope, we would need to create requests methods for all METHODS in `MetadataRequester.__init__` and follow through in many places of the code, especially `MetadataRequester.__getattr__`.
- [ ] MultiOutput* and RANSACRegressor still use `sample_weight` in their fit signatures and we can deprectate them now: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/34966#issuecomment-6190743248

Comments and feedback welcome here, @adrinjalali and @OmarManzoor. :)
Also CC @scikit-learn/core-devs in case that's of interest to someone else.

### Introduce yourself

_No response_

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

Attaching two ProgressBar instances on the same estimator breaks on teardown when the second one tries to `_run_queues.pop(context.root_uuid)`. 

I see two options to address the issue:

- Adding an attribute (maybe named `_unique`) to indicate that a callback can only have one instance attached to an estimator, and raising a `ValueError` if multiple are given to `set_callbacks`. This would also help the management of default callbacks in #34272 to ignore a default callback if one of the same unique callback was manually attached.

- Constraining all callback classes to work when multiple instances are attached to the same estimator and fix `ProgressBar` to do so. 

I have a preference for the first option, but I'd love to hear others' opinions.

ping @jeremiedbb @ogrisel

```python
from sklearn.callback.tests._utils import MaxIterEstimator

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

Attaching two ProgressBar instances on the same estimator breaks on teardown when the second one tries to `_run_queues.pop(context.root_uuid)`. 

I see two options to address the issue:

- Adding an attribute (maybe named `_unique`) to indicate that a callback can only have one instance attached to an estimator, and raising a `ValueError` if multiple are given to `set_callbacks`. This would also help the management of default callbacks in #34272 to ignore a default callback if one of the same unique callback was manually attached.

- Constraining all callback classes to work when multiple instances are attached to the same estimator and fix `ProgressBar` to do so. 

I have a preference for the first option, but I'd love to hear others' opinions.

_ACA Where do we want to use `sample_weight` by default?_

With #31413 ~~soon to be~~ merged, we have defined the mechanism for the auto-routing strategy in scikit-learn (and for use in third party libraries). It will be easily possible to define per estimator which methods of the estimator will request which metadata if users set `set_config(enable_metadata_requests=True)`. (Context: At one point in the future this setting will become the default, but for now it is opt-in.)

The way to do this is to call `add_auto_request` inside an estimator's `get_metadata_routing` method:

```py
class XYZEstimator(BaseEstimator):

    def get_metadata_routing(self):
        ...
        requests.fit.add_auto_request("sample_weight") # <--- one-liner to add auto-requests
        ...
```

The effect of adding an auto-request is that then `XYZEstimator.fit()` automatically requests and uses `sample_weight` if the user has passed it into the top-level meta-estimator or cross validation.

This issue is to define the scope of the auto-requests. 

We have discussed this in our bi-weekly meeting on pushing the subject of auto-requests and here we want to give everybody who is interested the opportunity to share their ideas on the following questions:

- Which metadata should get auto-requested ("sample_weigh", "X_val", "sample_weight_val", custom metadata, other?)
- Should we add auto-requests to `fit` and `score` everywhere or are there estimators where that doesn't make any sense?
- Which type of tests do we need?

My personal take would be to work these questions out in separate POC PRs.

CC @scikit-learn/core-devs for gathering opinions. I'm especially interested in the opinions of the statistically more inclined core devs (since we can figure out the engineering part pretty easily). Happy to discuss this in calls also.

### Describe the bug

`BaseRandomProjection.fit` ends with `self._n_features_out = self.n_components`. With the default `n_components="auto"` this stores the string `"auto"` instead of the inferred `n_components_`. > [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Background

This is the result of a discussion with @ogrisel and @jeremiedbb, fleshed out and with some additional ideas. I make my suggestion at the end, but will require feedback before I do any of the work.

### The problem

When using a container on Linux (Docker, Kubernetes, anything using cgroups), you can set a CPU quota, something like "this process gets 2 cores worth of compute."

Unfortunately, not all third-party C libraries know this. At minimum OpenBLAS does not seem to know about this limit (). So if you have 64 core machine, and run a Kubernetes pod with 8 cores, and OpenBLAS will think it has 64 cores, and it will be much much slower. Similarly libgomp and libomp. MKL builds on OpenMP so maybe no point in filing there until libgomp/libomp are fixed.

* https://github.com/OpenMathLib/OpenBLAS/issues/6059
* https://gcc.gnu.org/bugzilla/show_bug.cgi?id=127651
* https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/issues/225493

This is a performance problem for scikit-lean users.

### Demonstration

My CPU has 12 cores. I set up a cgroup with equivalent of 2 cores, but OpenBLAS still reports 12 cores:

```
$ systemd-run --user --scope --property CPUQuota="200%" -- python -c "import threadpoolctl; import numpy; print(threadpoolctl.ThreadpoolController().lib_controllers[0].get_num_threads())"
12
```

### Potential fixes

I am going to be fixing one case as a side-effect of https://github.com/joblib/joblib/issues/1846: when using `joblib.Parallel`, the number of cores will be constrained using `threadpoolctl`, including in sequential cases. However, this is a strange fix where if you don't use `joblib`, you still have the same performance problem.

So what else can be done until OpenBLAS any other relevant libraries fix this issue?

#### Option 1: joblib or scikit-learn set the limit correctly, on import

Instead of doing this in `Parallel` in the sequential case, do it on import of `joblib` or maybe `sklearn`: `threadpoolctl.threadpool_limits(limits=joblib.effective_cpu_count(-1))`.  (Technically this won't fix the above example because of https://github.com/joblib/loky/issues/634 but it will work in Docker or Kubernetes, and everywhere once that issue is fixed).

Pros:

* Fixes the limit for all use cases.

Cons:

* Importing a library changing global configuration. This is not very nice.

#### Option 2: sklearn sets the limit whenever calling into OpenMP or OpenBLAS

Pros:

* If you do `with threadpoolctl.threadpool_limits(limits=joblib.effective_cpu_count(-1))` it undoes the limits when done, so it's not a _permanent_ global config change, it's just DTRT.

Cons:

* This adds performance overhead of all these calls.
* Lots of code changes.

#### Option 3: Documentation of the problem and how to solve it

Pros:

* No impacts on global behavior.

Cons:

* Most people won't notice the documentation.
* If the situation improves or changes, most people won't re-read the updated docs.

#### Option 4: Warn on import

If `os.process_cpu_count() > joblib.effective_cpu_count(-1)` then that means cgroups is restricting CPU count further, so warn the user and tell them what to do. In practice should probably also docs to explain in more detail.

Pros:

* More likely to be noticed than docs.

Cons:

* Users will still have to do work.

### My suggestion

After further thought, I think setting the limit on import (option 1) is actually reasonable. The hope is that this is a stop-gap and can eventually be removed once the relevant libraries DTRT, and in practice for the vast majority of people this is the right thing to do.

If that's not acceptable, docs + warning is what I would suggest doing.

I can proceed with either, once there is some consensus.

* If you do `with threadpoolctl.threadpool_limits(limits=joblib.effective_cpu_count(-1))` it undoes the limits when done, so it's not a _permanent_ global config change, it's just DTRT.

Cons:

* This adds performance overhead of all these calls.
* Lots of code changes.

#### Option 3: Documentation of the problem and how to solve it

Pros:

* No impacts on global behavior.

Cons:

* Most people won't notice the documentation.
* If the situation improves or changes, most people won't re-read the updated docs.

#### Option 4: Warn on import

If `os.process_cpu_count() > joblib.effective_cpu_count(-1)` then that means cgroups is restricting CPU count further, so warn the user and tell them what to do. In practice should probably also docs to explain in more detail.

Pros:

* More likely to be noticed than docs.

Cons:

* Users will still have to do work.

### My suggestion

After further thought, I think setting the limit on import (option 1) is actually reasonable. The hope is that this is a stop-gap and can eventually be removed once the relevant libraries DTRT, and in practice for the vast majority of people this is the right thing to do.

If that's not acceptable, docs + warning is what I would suggest doing.

> [!WARNING] > This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label. ### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact scikit-learn's linear models split into two families with very different handling of un-centered features: - `LinearRegression`, `Ridge`, `Lasso`, `ElasticNet` go through `_preprocess_data`, which centers `X` and `y` (explicitly for dense data, algebraically for sparse) before solving, then reconstructs the intercept afterward. Centering is a pure reparametrization here: for any fixed `coef`, shifting `X` by a constant only shifts the intercept, and the L1/L2 penalty doesn't touch the intercept, so the optimal `coef` is mathematically invariant to any additive shift of the features. Ridge/Lasso exploit this to shield users from poor numerical stability on high mean to variance ratio features. - `LogisticRegression`, `PoissonRegressor`, `GammaRegressor`, `TweedieRegressor` (the `LinearModelLoss` + `NewtonSolver`/lbfgs/newton-cg/newton-cholesky family) do **not** do this. The intercept is just another free parameter solved jointly with the coefficients directly on the raw `X`. There is no `_preprocess_data`-equivalent step. The same invariance holds mathematically for this second family too (same argument: additive shift + unpenalized intercept), but because nothing centers the data first, the solvers can lose that invariance numerically. Concretely: - `newton-cholesky` builds its Hessian from the raw `[X, 1]` design. Eliminating the intercept column during Cholesky factorization implicitly computes `X.T @ X - n * mean(X) * mean(X).T` which can yield catastrophic-cancellation-prone quantity. The scipy solver normally fires a warning or an error in this case, so at least, it's visible for users something is wrong. - `lbfgs` doesn't have a cancellation problem in this sense, but its gradient-norm convergence check can be satisfied prematurely on badly-offset data, silently stopping far from the true optimum, with **no warning at all**. User-facing impact: any real dataset with a feature that's far from zero-mean relative to its variance (a year, a timestamp, an age, a physical measurement with an offset unit) can silently produce badly wrong `coef_`/`intercept_` for these estimators, without any indication something went wrong. I stumbled on this while investigating numerical-stability discussions in #34793 (Ridge's cholesky centering trick). ### Steps/Code to Reproduce Sweep used to generate the plot below:
```python import warnings import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from sklearn.linear_model import ( LinearRegression, LogisticRegression, Ridge, TweedieRegressor, PoissonRegressor, ElasticNet, ) def relative_error_vs_mean_variance_ratio( linear_estimator, dtype="float32", random_seed=0, max_ratio=1e5 ): rng = np.random.RandomState(random_seed) n_samples, n_features = 5000, 5 X = rng.normal(size=(n_samples, n_features)) true_coef = rng.normal(size=n_features) proba = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(X @ true_coef))) y = (rng.uniform(size=n_samples) < proba).astype(int) X, y = X.astype(dtype), y.astype(dtype) linear_estimator.fit(X, y) ref = linear_estimator.coef_.copy() assert np.linalg.norm(ref) > 0.1 # we want coefs that aren't too small ratios = np.logspace(0, np.log10(max_ratio), num=30) errors, has_warnings = [], [] for offset in ratios: with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught: linear_estimator.fit((X + offset).astype(dtype), y) shifted = linear_estimator.coef_.copy() errors.append(np.linalg.norm(shifted - ref) / np.linalg.norm(ref)) has_warnings.append(bool(caught)) return ratios, np.array(errors), np.array(has_warnings) models = [ Ridge(solver="cholesky", alpha=1 / 5000), Ridge(solver="lbfgs", positive=True, alpha=1 / 5000), ElasticNet(alpha=1 / 5000), LinearRegression(), # GLMs: LogisticRegression(solver="lbfgs"), LogisticRegression(solver="newton-cholesky"), TweedieRegressor(solver="lbfgs", alpha=1 / 5000), TweedieRegressor(solver="newton-cholesky", alpha=1 / 5000), PoissonRegressor(solver="lbfgs", alpha=1 / 5000), PoissonRegressor(solver="newton-cholesky", alpha=1 / 5000), ] dtypes = ["float32", "float64"] n_cols = 2 n_rows = -(-len(models) // n_cols) # ceil division fig, axes = plt.subplots( n_rows, n_cols, figsize=(5 * n_cols, 3 * n_rows), sharex=True, sharey=True ) axes = axes.ravel() for ax, model in zip(axes, models): results = [relative_error_vs_mean_variance_ratio(model, dtype=dtype) for dtype in dtypes] for (ratios, errors, has_warnings), dtype in zip(results, dtypes): line, = ax.plot(ratios, errors, label=dtype) ax.scatter( ratios[has_warnings], errors[has_warnings], marker="x", s=10, color=line.get_color(), ) ax.set_ylim(0, 1.02) ax.set_xscale("log") ax.set_title(str(model), fontsize=9) ax.tick_params(axis="x", which="both", labelbottom=True) ax.set_xlabel("mean/variance ratio") for ax in axes[len(models):]: ax.axis("off") for ax in axes[::n_cols]: ax.set_ylabel("relative error") axes[0].legend() fig.tight_layout() ```
### Expected Results Fitting on `X + offset` should not change `coef_` (more than floating point noise) or at the very least should not change `coef_` without a warning. ### Actual Results The grid below (generated by the reproducer snippet) sweeps the feature mean/variance ratio (`X + ratio`, unit-variance `X`) from 1 to 1e5, one subplot per estimator, and plots the relative error of `coef_` against the ratio=0 reference, for both `float32` and `float64`, with `×` marking points where a warning was raised: - `Ridge`, `LinearRegression`, `ElasticNet` (top two rows, the `_preprocess_data` family): error stays ~0 across the entire range, in both dtypes. A blip only appears in float32 at the extreme end (ratio ≥1e4), never in float64. - `LogisticRegression`, `TweedieRegressor`, `PoissonRegressor` (bottom three rows, the GLM family), with *either* solver (lbfgs or newton-cholesky): garbage coefficients starting at a ratio as low as ~20-100 in float32 and ~300-5000 in float64. ### Versions ```shell System: python: 3.14.6 (main, Jun 23 2026, 15:18:23) [Clang 22.1.3 ] executable: /home/arthur/scikit-learn/sklearn-env/bin/python machine: Linux-6.17.0-1032-oem-x86_64-with-glibc2.39 Python dependencies: sklearn: 1.10.dev0 pip: None setuptools: None numpy: 2.5.3 scipy: 1.18.1 Cython: 3.3.0 pandas: 3.0.5 matplotlib: 3.11.1 joblib: 1.6.0 threadpoolctl: 3.6.0 narwhals: 2.26.0 Built with OpenMP: True threadpoolctl info: user_api: blas internal_api: openblas num_threads: 14 prefix: libscipy_openblas filepath: /home/arthur/scikit-learn/sklearn-env/lib/python3.14/site-packages/numpy.libs/libscipy_openblas64_-f48b354e.so version: 0.3.34.106.0 threading_layer: pthreads architecture: Haswell user_api: blas internal_api: openblas num_threads: 14 prefix: libscipy_openblas filepath: /home/arthur/scikit-learn/sklearn-env/lib/python3.14/site-packages/scipy.libs/libscipy_openblas-5f890258.so version: 0.3.31.dev threading_layer: pthreads architecture: Haswell user_api: openmp internal_api: openmp num_threads: 14 prefix: libgomp filepath: /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libgomp.so.1.0.0 version: None ``` ### Interest in fixing the bug Yes. I'm about to open a PR with a proposed fixed: detecting high mean/variance ratio and explicitly recentering if needed.

### Introduce yourself

Hello, I am using sklearn for the forecasting project and in the meantime found some issues I reported here. 

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

`HistGradientBoostingRegressor` and `HistGradientBoostingClassifier` accept explicit `X_val` and `y_val` but do not enable early stopping with `early_stopping="auto"` on a small training set. This also affects calls that leave `early_stopping` at its default value, `"auto"`.

In the example below, both estimators fit successfully on 30 training samples, but `do_early_stopping_` is `False` and `validation_score_` is empty. Changing only `early_stopping` to `True` enables monitoring of the same validation data and records four validation scores.

The user-facing problem is that the supplied validation data does not participate in the early-stopping checks, despite the documented automatic activation. This is not just missing score history: the validation-based stopping criterion is disabled. In longer runs, this could cause unnecessary boosting iterations and potentially affect generalization. The example establishes disabled monitoring and stopping checks; it does not establish degraded predictions or a production incident.

A workaround is to set `early_stopping=True` explicitly when providing validation arrays.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
import sklearn
from sklearn.ensemble import (
    HistGradientBoostingClassifier,
    HistGradientBoostingRegressor,
)

print(sklearn.__version__)
X = np.arange(40.0).reshape(-1, 1)

for estimator_class in (
    HistGradientBoostingRegressor,
    HistGradientBoostingClassifier,
):
    y = (
        np.sin(X[:, 0])
        if estimator_class is HistGradientBoostingRegressor
        else np.arange(40) % 2
    )
    for mode in ("auto", True):
        estimator = estimator_class(
            early_stopping=mode, max_iter=3, random_state=0
        ).fit(X[:30], y[:30], X_val=X[30:], y_val=y[30:])
        print(
            estimator_class.__name__, mode,
            estimator.do_early_stopping_,
            len(estimator.validation_score_),
        )
```

### Expected Results

With explicit validation arrays, both modes should enable early stopping for both estimators, even with only 30 training samples:

```text
1.9.0
HistGradientBoostingRegressor auto True 4
HistGradientBoostingRegressor True True 4
HistGradientBoostingClassifier auto True 4
HistGradientBoostingClassifier True True 4
```

The version 1.9 documentation specifies automatic activation when either the training sample count exceeds 10,000 or `X_val` and `y_val` are supplied to `fit`:

- [HistGradientBoostingRegressor documentation](https://scikit-learn.org/1.9/modules/generated/sklearn.ensemble.HistGradientBoostingRegressor.html)
- [HistGradientBoostingClassifier documentation](https://scikit-learn.org/1.9/modules/generated/sklearn.ensemble.HistGradientBoostingClassifier.html)

Four scores correspond to the initial model plus three completed boosting iterations. The example tests whether validation monitoring is enabled, not whether fitting must terminate before `max_iter`.

### Actual Results

The reported run on scikit-learn 1.9.0 produced:

```text
1.9.0
HistGradientBoostingRegressor auto False 0
HistGradientBoostingRegressor True True 4
HistGradientBoostingClassifier auto False 0
HistGradientBoostingClassifier True True 4
```

No exception is raised. Automatic mode leaves early stopping disabled and records no validation scores, while explicit `True` monitors the same validation data.

### Versions

```shell
1.9.0
1.9.1
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

In [`BaseHistGradientBoosting.fit` at tag 1.9.0](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/1.9.0/sklearn/ensemble/_hist_gradient_boosting/gradient_boosting.py), the automatic-mode decision only checks the training sample count:

```python
if self.early_stopping == "auto":
    self.do_early_stopping_ = n_samples > 10_000
```

The method has already calculated `validation_data_provided` and checked that both validation arrays are supplied together, but that flag is not included in the automatic-mode decision.

A candidate fix is:

```diff
- self.do_early_stopping_ = n_samples > 10_000
+ self.do_early_stopping_ = n_samples > 10_000 or validation_data_provided
```

This is a source-based suggestion, not a tested patch.

A regression test should cover both estimator classes with a small training set, explicit validation arrays, and `early_stopping="auto"`, and check:

```python
assert estimator.do_early_stopping_
assert len(estimator.validation_score_) == estimator.n_iter_ + 1
```

Keep `early_stopping=True` as a passing control. Additional coverage should preserve the sample-count rule when validation arrays are absent, including the 10,000-sample boundary, and preserve the existing validation-argument errors.

Related work: [#18748](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/18748) requested custom validation-set support, and [#27124](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/27124) introduced the explicit validation arguments. These references do not establish that no duplicate report exists.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

`DecisionTree*.fit(X, y, check_input=False)` silently ignores missing values: with `check_input=False`, `_fit` skips `_compute_missing_values_in_feature_mask`, so `missing_values_in_feature_mask` stays `None` and the splitter treats NaNs as regular values. No error, no warning, just a wrong tree (NaN thresholds, spurious depth).

And there's no way around it from the public API: the mask can only be passed to the private `_fit`. That's what forests do (they compute the mask once and pass it to each tree via `tree._fit(..., check_input=False, missing_values_in_feature_mask=...)`).

Within scikit-learn, the only caller of the public `fit(..., check_input=False)` is `BaseGradientBoosting` (`_gb.py`), which is safe only because it rejects NaNs upfront. So this mostly affects third-party code using `check_input=False` (which the docstring discourages: "Don't use this parameter unless you know what you're doing").

More broadly, a single boolean isn't enough to express "this input was already validated" for trees anymore: callers also need to provide the missing-values mask (and, with categorical support, the encoding info). Possible ways forward:

1. **Compute the mask even when `check_input=False`** on the public `fit` (when none is provided). It's one pass over `X`, cheap compared to building a tree, and makes the result correct.
2. **Document** that missing values aren't supported with `check_input=False`. Cheap, but leaves a silent trap.
3. **Deprecate `check_input` in the public `fit`** of trees, and switch gradient boosting to `_fit` (like forests). With 1. applied during the deprecation cycle.

I'd go with 3.

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

X = np.array([[0.0], [1.0], [np.nan], [np.nan], [2.0], [3.0]], dtype=np.float32)
y = np.array([0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0])

    tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0).fit(X, y, check_input=check_input)
    print(f"{check_input=}: depth={tree.get_depth()}, thresholds={tree.tree_.threshold}")
```

Same tree for both (or at least an error for `check_input=False`):

check_input=True: depth=1, thresholds=[inf -2. -2.]

> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

Hi, I’m Luis. I’m starting to contribute to scikit-learn by working through focused issues in its Bayesian linear models. I noticed this behavior while investigating `ARDRegression` after the discussion on #35026, and wanted to report a reproducible example before proposing a change.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

With `compute_score=True`, `ARDRegression` computes the posterior covariance and coefficients, updates `alpha_` and `lambda_`, then calculates `scores_` using the **updated precisions** but the **previous covariance and residual sum of squares**. As a result, the last score can differ from the objective evaluated at the fitted parameters. This can mislead users who inspect `scores_` to monitor optimization or compare the final score with an evaluation at the fitted parameters. Fitted coefficients and predictions appear unaffected

This is separate from whether the objective should include normalization constants: the comparison below omits the same constants as the current implementation.

If `scores_[-1]` is intended to report the objective at the fitted parameters, its covariance, coefficients, residuals, and precisions should correspond to the same parameter state.

There is also a related question for pruning: once the active feature set is stable, the determinant uses the covariance of retained features, while the score sums `log(lambda_)` over **all** features. Should the score represent evidence for the retained-feature model, or a limiting form of the full model? Clarifying that definition would help determine the appropriate treatment of pruned features.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import ARDRegression

rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
X = rng.normal(size=(12, 4))
y = X @ np.array([1.2, -0.5, 0.0, 0.8]) + rng.normal(
    scale=0.3, size=12
)

reg = ARDRegression(
    max_iter=1,
    compute_score=True,
    fit_intercept=False,
    threshold_lambda=1e12,
    alpha_1=0.2,
    alpha_2=0.3,
    lambda_1=0.7,
    lambda_2=1.2,
).fit(X, y)

alpha, lam = reg.alpha_, reg.lambda_
A = np.diag(lam) + alpha * (X.T @ X)
mu = alpha * np.linalg.solve(A, X.T @ y)
sse = np.sum((y - X @ mu) ** 2)

score_at_fitted_parameters = (
    (reg.lambda_1 * np.log(lam) - reg.lambda_2 * lam).sum()
    + reg.alpha_1 * np.log(alpha)
    - reg.alpha_2 * alpha
    + 0.5 * (
        -np.linalg.slogdet(A)[1]
        + X.shape[0] * np.log(alpha)
        + np.log(lam).sum()
        - alpha * sse
        - np.sum(lam * mu**2)
    )
)

print(reg.scores_[-1])
print(score_at_fitted_parameters)
```

With scikit-learn 1.8.0, this prints approximately `-5.488435` and `-7.335993`. No features are pruned in this example. The calculations use the same unnormalized objective, so omitted constants do not explain the difference.

### Expected Results

The final `scores_` entry should equal the objective evaluated at the fitted `alpha_` and `lambda_`. For this reproducer, that value is approximately `-7.335993011208482`. Each score should use the posterior and precisions from the same iteration.

### Actual Results

With scikit-learn 1.8.0, the reproducer prints:

```text
-5.48843505092349
-7.335993011208482
```

The first value is `reg.scores_[-1]`; the second is the objective recomputed at the fitted parameters. They differ by approximately `1.847558`.

### Introduce yourself

Hi, I’m Luis. I’m starting to contribute to scikit-learn by working through focused issues in its Bayesian linear models. I noticed this behavior while investigating `ARDRegression` after the discussion on #35026, and wanted to report a reproducible example before proposing a change.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

With `compute_score=True`, `ARDRegression` computes the posterior covariance and coefficients, updates `alpha_` and `lambda_`, then calculates `scores_` using the **updated precisions** but the **previous covariance and residual sum of squares**. As a result, the last score can differ from the objective evaluated at the fitted parameters. This can mislead users who inspect `scores_` to monitor optimization or compare the final score with an evaluation at the fitted parameters. Fitted coefficients and predictions appear unaffected

This is separate from whether the objective should include normalization constants: the comparison below omits the same constants as the current implementation.

If `scores_[-1]` is intended to report the objective at the fitted parameters, its covariance, coefficients, residuals, and precisions should correspond to the same parameter state.

There is also a related question for pruning: once the active feature set is stable, the determinant uses the covariance of retained features, while the score sums `log(lambda_)` over **all** features. Should the score represent evidence for the retained-feature model, or a limiting form of the full model? Clarifying that definition would help determine the appropriate treatment of pruned features.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import ARDRegression

rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
X = rng.normal(size=(12, 4))
y = X @ np.array([1.2, -0.5, 0.0, 0.8]) + rng.normal(
    scale=0.3, size=12
)

reg = ARDRegression(
    max_iter=1,
    compute_score=True,
    fit_intercept=False,
    threshold_lambda=1e12,
    alpha_1=0.2,
    alpha_2=0.3,
    lambda_1=0.7,
    lambda_2=1.2,
).fit(X, y)

alpha, lam = reg.alpha_, reg.lambda_
A = np.diag(lam) + alpha * (X.T @ X)
mu = alpha * np.linalg.solve(A, X.T @ y)
sse = np.sum((y - X @ mu) ** 2)

score_at_fitted_parameters = (
    (reg.lambda_1 * np.log(lam) - reg.lambda_2 * lam).sum()
    + reg.alpha_1 * np.log(alpha)
    - reg.alpha_2 * alpha
    + 0.5 * (
        -np.linalg.slogdet(A)[1]
        + X.shape[0] * np.log(alpha)
        + np.log(lam).sum()
        - alpha * sse
        - np.sum(lam * mu**2)
    )
)

print(reg.scores_[-1])
print(score_at_fitted_parameters)
```

With scikit-learn 1.8.0, this prints approximately `-5.488435` and `-7.335993`. No features are pruned in this example. The calculations use the same unnormalized objective, so omitted constants do not explain the difference.

### Expected Results

The final `scores_` entry should equal the objective evaluated at the fitted `alpha_` and `lambda_`. For this reproducer, that value is approximately `-7.335993011208482`. Each score should use the posterior and precisions from the same iteration.

### Actual Results

With scikit-learn 1.8.0, the reproducer prints:

```text
-5.48843505092349
-7.335993011208482
```

The first value is `reg.scores_[-1]`; the second is the objective recomputed at the fitted parameters. They differ by approximately `1.847558`.

body_text:
On free-threaded Python, a lock that many threads take at the same time can make thread-parallel code collapse on a machine with hundreds of cores, while the same code looks fine on a laptop. I hit this with random forests. I'm opening this issue to share what I found, discuss how to avoid it in scikit-learn, and track the related work.

#### How I got here

As you might know, I'm benchmarking scikit-learn on several machines, one of them is a 2 x 86-core Xeon 6787P (344 hardware threads).

On this machine, random forests fitted with 344 threads (what you get with `n_jobs=-1`) were often slower on free-threaded 3.14 than with the GIL (median 0.45x over 31 representative benchmark cases). For instance, the reproducer below takes ~3s with the GIL and ~12s free-threaded.

With gdb, I first found most threads parked on CPython's `LOAD_GLOBAL` specialization lock (python/cpython#152075, fixed on CPython `main`).

Then I saw the same collapse on other locks, taken once per tree:

- the `sys.modules` lookups of function-level imports and the `lru_cache` behind `inspect.getattr_static`, both from narwhals' dataframe checks in `check_array`;
- the `warnings` module lock, taken by the per-task warning filters handling of `sklearn.utils.parallel`.

The slowdown always appeared suddenly past a few tens of threads. This comes from CPython's locks (python/cpython#158901): once a thread has waited more than 1 ms, each lock acquisition costs a thread wake-up, so the waits get longer and the lock never gets back to the fast path. On a 14 or 16-core laptop this threshold is barely reached, so nothing shows.

#### Reproducer

```python
import time

from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.ensemble import ExtraTreesClassifier

X, y = make_classification(n_samples=100_000, n_features=20, random_state=0)
clf = ExtraTreesClassifier(n_estimators=688, n_jobs=-1, random_state=0)
tic = time.perf_counter()
clf.fit(X, y)
print(f"fit: {time.perf_counter() - tic:.2f} s")
```

Fit time on the 2 x 86-core Xeon 6787P, 3 runs, one fresh process per run:

| | GIL (3.14.7) | free-threaded (3.14.7t) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `main` (6ad9bb9ed6) | 2.2 to 3.3 s | 12.3 to 13.0 s |
| cakedev0/scikit-learn#19 | 1.7 to 1.9 s | 0.70 to 0.74 s |

#### What fixed it for forests

cakedev0/scikit-learn#19 makes the reproducer 17x faster free-threaded:

- Trees are fitted with a thread pool that starts its threads lazily, one per task (`ThreadPoolExecutor`, through the `_parallel_thread_map` of #34914). The threads start a bit apart, so they rarely take the same lock at the same time. joblib's threading backend starts all its workers before dispatching, so they run the same code in lockstep. With the GIL it's the opposite: starting the workers first is faster, so the thread pool does that only when the GIL is enabled.
- Trees don't validate again the inputs already validated by the forest (`check_input=False` no longer calls `check_array` per tree).
- `sklearn.utils.parallel` no longer resets the warning filters in each task (now in its own issue and PR: #35089, #35090). This also fixes a race on GIL Python with threads: the user's warning filters could be silently lost, and spurious "`delayed` should be used with `Parallel`" warnings raised.

#### What to watch for

Code that runs in many threads at the same time should avoid process-wide locks in each task. The ones I found:

- `warnings.catch_warnings()` and changes of the warning filters;
- `functools.lru_cache`'d functions (cache hits included), including stdlib ones like `inspect.getattr_static`;
- `import` statements inside functions;
- `isinstance` checks against an ABC, true or false, including `scipy.sparse.issparse` (`isinstance(x, SparseABC)`): the ABC's caches are sets shared by all threads, and each lookup takes the set's lock. So every `issparse(ndarray)` call from every thread goes through one `PyMutex`;
- input validation (`check_array` and its narwhals checks): validate once, before the parallel loop.

Benchmarks on 16 cores can hide a 10x to 100x collapse. Close to the threshold, timings are also bimodal (4.8 to 9.6 s for the same fit at 344 threads), so repeats are needed.

Note for benchmarks: measure warm fits too (several fits in one process), not only fresh processes. On free-threaded Python, the `LOAD_GLOBAL` specialization contention is paid by the first fit only: on `main`, the reproducer's first fit takes 10 to 12 s, the next ones ~4 s.

Thread-based parallelism in scikit-learn today: forests (`fit`, `predict`, `apply`, `decision_path`), `IsolationForest`, `neighbors` queries, `pairwise_distances`, SGD one-vs-all, coordinate descent paths, HGB binning, and `LogisticRegression` free-threaded.

#### Tracking

Upstream:

- [ ] `LOAD_GLOBAL` specialization contention: python/cpython#152075 (fixed on CPython `main`, backported to 3.14 in python/cpython#158904, 3.15 backport in python/cpython#158905)
- [ ] `PyMutex` fair handoff makes contention collapse: python/cpython#158901
- [ ] joblib's threading backend overhead: joblib/joblib#1830
- [ ] narwhals' dataframe checks contend (mostly `inspect.getattr_static`): not reported yet, depends on python/cpython#158901
- [ ] `issparse` contends on the ABC cache of `SparseABC`: not reported yet. Seen with gdb on `test_partial_dependence_non_null_weight_idx` with `--parallel-threads 14` (all but one thread waiting in `issparse` from `Tree.apply`), once the `warnings` lock contention was removed. A fast path in `issparse` for exact types (scipy) or lock-free ABC cache lookups (CPython) would avoid it
- [x] `multiprocessing.pool.ThreadPool.terminate()` doesn't join its threads: already reported in python/cpython#107616, no performance impact seen

scikit-learn:

- Forests (cakedev0/scikit-learn#19):
  - [ ] lazy thread pool: should be less needed once python/cpython#152075 is in. With `PYTHON_TLBC=0` as a stand-in for that fix, joblib was still 1.5x to 4x slower on 344 threads with fast-to-build trees (0.1 to 1 s each). The gap shrinks for slow-to-build trees (~1.1x for year_prediction_msd).
  - [ ] no per-tree validation (works around the narwhals contention, and saves a `check_array` per tree)
- [ ] Warning filters race/lock in `sklearn.utils.parallel` (bug on `main`): #35089, fixed by #35090
- [ ] Audit the other thread-parallel code paths on a many-core machine (list above)
- [ ] Write down what to watch for, for contributors (see #34596)

#### Related issues

- #30007
- #20666

### Introduce yourself

_No response_

### Describe the workflow you want to enable

We use Isotonic regression to calibrate scores on a log-odds / log-likelihood-ratio scale. On such scales, the extreme values are naturally +inf / -inf (e.g., probabilities of exactly 0 or 1). IsotonicRegression.fit currently rejects these inputs:
```
import numpy as np
from sklearn.isotonic import IsotonicRegression

ir = IsotonicRegression()
ir.fit([0.0, 1.0, np.inf], [0.0, 0.5, 1.0])
# ValueError: Input X contains infinity or a value too large for dtype('float64')
```

However, the algorithm itself can support `inf` values without a problem. The Error is raised by `check_array`, which has `ensure_all_finite=False`.

### Describe your proposed solution

Relax the validation in `check_array` to allow for `(-)inf`, but add a check for NaNs (e.g. `np.any(np.isnan(X))`) that raises a ValueError.



### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

_No response_

### Additional context

Versions: scikit-learn 1.7.2, Python 3.14.

If this change is something that is desirable, I can create a PR for it myself.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

Since the callbacks API (#33322), a parallel `GridSearchCV` with many cheap fits is much slower than in 1.8. On a 2000-candidate grid on iris (10k fits of ~1 ms), `n_jobs=8` takes ~3 s on 1.8.0 but 100-150 s on 1.9.1 and 24-67 s on main. That's much slower than `n_jobs=1` (~9 s). No callback is registered.

`BaseSearchCV.fit` creates one `CallbackContext` per (candidate, split) up front and passes one to each `_fit_and_score` task. `subcontext` registers the child in the parent's `_children_map` and sets `child.parent`, so pickling one task's context pickles its parent and every sibling. The pickled task grows linearly with the number of tasks: ~50 KB per task for 500 tasks, ~420 KB per task for 5000 tasks (measured on main by pickling the `delayed` arguments `BaseSearchCV.fit` builds).

joblib pickles each batch separately, so the total pickling work is roughly (number of batches) x (number of tasks). Auto-batching hides part of it because a batch shares the pickle memo. With `pre_dispatch="all"` (batches of one task) and `refit=False`, the search takes 290 s on main, and 4.6 s with the contexts left out of the tasks.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import time

from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

X, y = load_iris(return_X_y=True)
param_grid = {"max_depth": range(1, 21), "random_state": range(100)}  # 2000 candidates

for n_jobs in [1, 8]:
    search = GridSearchCV(DecisionTreeClassifier(), param_grid, cv=5, n_jobs=n_jobs)
    tic = time.perf_counter()
    search.fit(X, y)
    print(f"n_jobs={n_jobs}: {time.perf_counter() - tic:.1f}s")
```

### Expected Results

Same as 1.8.0:

```
n_jobs=1: 8.7s
n_jobs=8: 3.1s
```

### Actual Results

1.9.1:

```
n_jobs=1: 10.9s
n_jobs=8: 105.9s
```

`n_jobs=8` varies a lot between runs: 100.6 s, 105.9 s and 151.1 s on 1.9.1, and 23.8 s, 31.9 s and 67.2 s on main. 1.8.0 is stable at 3.0-3.1 s. Intel Core Ultra 5 225H (14 cores), same Python and joblib for all three.

### Versions

```shell
System:
    python: 3.13.14 (main, Jun 23 2026, 15:18:27) [Clang 22.1.3 ]
   machine: Linux-6.17.0-1032-oem-x86_64-with-glibc2.39

Python dependencies:
      sklearn: 1.9.1
        numpy: 2.5.3
        scipy: 1.18.1
       joblib: 1.6.0
threadpoolctl: 3.7.0
     narwhals: 2.26.0

Built with OpenMP: True
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

`BaseSearchCV.fit` creates one `CallbackContext` per (candidate, split) up front and passes one to each `_fit_and_score` task. `subcontext` registers the child in the parent's `_children_map` and sets `child.parent`, so pickling one task's context pickles its parent and every sibling. The pickled task grows linearly with the number of tasks: ~50 KB per task for 500 tasks, ~420 KB per task for 5000 tasks (measured on main by pickling the `delayed` arguments `BaseSearchCV.fit` builds).

joblib pickles each batch separately, so the total pickling work is roughly (number of batches) x (number of tasks). Auto-batching hides part of it because a batch shares the pickle memo. With `pre_dispatch="all"` (batches of one task) and `refit=False`, the search takes 290 s on main, and 4.6 s with the contexts left out of the tasks.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import time

from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

X, y = load_iris(return_X_y=True)
param_grid = {"max_depth": range(1, 21), "random_state": range(100)}  # 2000 candidates

for n_jobs in [1, 8]:
    search = GridSearchCV(DecisionTreeClassifier(), param_grid, cv=5, n_jobs=n_jobs)
    tic = time.perf_counter()
    search.fit(X, y)
    print(f"n_jobs={n_jobs}: {time.perf_counter() - tic:.1f}s")
```

### Expected Results

Same as 1.8.0:

```
n_jobs=1: 8.7s
n_jobs=8: 3.1s
```

### Actual Results

1.9.1:

```
n_jobs=1: 10.9s
n_jobs=8: 105.9s
```

`n_jobs=8` varies a lot between runs: 100.6 s, 105.9 s and 151.1 s on 1.9.1, and 23.8 s, 31.9 s and 67.2 s on main. 1.8.0 is stable at 3.0-3.1 s. Intel Core Ultra 5 225H (14 cores), same Python and joblib for all three.

from threading import Barrier

from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, RobustScaler

if '--preimport' in sys.argv:
    import pandas

X, y = load_iris(return_X_y=True)
barrier = Barrier(4)

def fit_one(i):
    preprocessor = make_column_transformer(
        (StandardScaler(), [0, 2]), (RobustScaler(), [1, 3])
    )
    barrier.wait()
    sleep(i * 0.02)
    return preprocessor.fit_transform(X, y).shape

print('pandas imported before fits:', 'pandas' in sys.modules)
with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as pool:
    for future in [pool.submit(fit_one, i) for i in range(4)]:
        print(future.result())
```

### Note

- one work-around is to `import pandas` early
- this is not free-threaded specific

### Codex claims (not double-checked yet)

1. One thread finishes the preprocessing steps and reaches [`ColumnTransformer._validate_output`](/home/lesteve/dev/scikit-learn/sklearn/compose/_column_transformer.py:753), which imports pandas—even when inputs and outputs are NumPy arrays.
2. Python puts the pandas module into `sys.modules` **before its initialization finishes**. [Python import documentation](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/import.html#loading)
3. Another thread validates feature names through [`_get_feature_names`](/home/lesteve/dev/scikit-learn/sklearn/utils/validation.py:2352). Narwhals’ `get_pandas()` reads `sys.modules` directly, then accesses `pd.DataFrame`, which does not exist yet.

That direct lookup bypasses import synchronization. The “most likely due to a circular import” text is misleading here: this is a concurrent import race.

print('pandas imported before fits:', 'pandas' in sys.modules)
with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as pool:
    for future in [pool.submit(fit_one, i) for i in range(4)]:
        print(future.result())

### Note

- one work-around is to `import pandas` early
- this is not free-threaded specific

### Codex claims (not double-checked yet)

1. One thread finishes the preprocessing steps and reaches [`ColumnTransformer._validate_output`](/home/lesteve/dev/scikit-learn/sklearn/compose/_column_transformer.py:753), which imports pandas—even when inputs and outputs are NumPy arrays.
2. Python puts the pandas module into `sys.modules` **before its initialization finishes**. [Python import documentation](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/import.html#loading)
3. Another thread validates feature names through [`_get_feature_names`](/home/lesteve/dev/scikit-learn/sklearn/utils/validation.py:2352). Narwhals’ `get_pandas()` reads `sys.modules` directly, then accesses `pd.DataFrame`, which does not exist yet.

That direct lookup bypasses import synchronization. The “most likely due to a circular import” text is misleading here: this is a concurrent import race.

> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

_No response_

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

Related to https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/35109

When an estimator sets `feature_names_in_`, which happens whenever a DataFrame is passed to them for instance, the resulting estimator will not be movable to namespaces that do not support string arrays.

I am not aware of any way to fit an estimator on GPU to data with column names under the current array API design, but it feels logical that moving one such estimator that was fitted on CPU should be possible. Perhaps the features names could be dropped (since they will emit a warning when passing array data to methods like `.predict()`), or kept as-is, but my expectation is that moving the estimator should work without manual intervention on the object.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import os
os.environ["SCIPY_ARRAY_API"] = "1"

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=123)
X = rng.standard_normal(size=(20, 3))
y = rng.integers(2, size=X.shape[0])
df = pd.DataFrame(X)
df.columns = [f"col{cl}" for cl in range(X.shape[1])]

from sklearn import set_config
set_config(array_api_dispatch=True)

from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
model = LogisticRegression().fit(df, y)

from sklearn.utils._array_api import get_namespace_and_device, move_estimator_to
import torch
xp, _, device = get_namespace_and_device(torch.arange(1))
model_moved = move_estimator_to(model, xp=xp, device=device)
```

### Expected Results

Moved model, with the feature names either dropped or kept as numpy.

### Actual Results

```
TypeError: can't convert np.ndarray of type numpy.object_. The only supported types are: float64, float32, float16, complex64, complex128, int64, int32, int16, int8, uint64, uint32, uint16, uint8, and bool.
```

> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Describe the bug

On Covertype, `HistGradientBoostingClassifier` with **every hyperparameter at its default** (only `max_iter=200, early_stopping=False, random_state=0` set) reaches a minimum *training* log-loss of 0.418 at iteration 55, and then **rises**: 1.08 at iteration 100, 1.93 at 200. 87 of the 200 iterations increase the training loss, and leaf values reach 2.2e4. The fit is deterministic (a second fit is bit-identical) and gives identical numbers on aarch64 (AWS Graviton4) and x86. On the full dataset with `max_leaf_nodes=255` it goes 0.200 at iteration 40 → 0.817 at 100, with leaves reaching 5.7e4.

LightGBM 4.7.0 and XGBoost 3.4.2, configured through scikit-learn's own `get_equivalent_estimator` (l2 = 0; XGBoost's learning rate doubled for its 2p(1−p) hessian), decrease monotonically on the same rows, to 0.16 and 0.15.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import fetch_covtype
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import log_loss

X, y = fetch_covtype(return_X_y=True)
idx = np.random.default_rng(0).permutation(len(y))[:20000]
X, y = X[idx, :10], y[idx]            # 10 numeric features, 7 classes

m = HistGradientBoostingClassifier(max_iter=200, early_stopping=False, random_state=0).fit(X, y)
for k, p in enumerate(m.staged_predict_proba(X), 1):
    if k in (25, 50, 55, 100, 200):
        print(k, round(log_loss(y, p, labels=m.classes_), 4))
```

The exact script that produced the numbers here (it also does the parameter sweep and the LightGBM/XGBoost comparison) is [hgb_repro.py](https://github.com/scttfrdmn/scientific-codes-cookbook/blob/main/measurements/scikit-learn-real/hgb-repro/hgb_repro.py), and [hgb-repro.log](https://github.com/scttfrdmn/scientific-codes-cookbook/blob/main/measurements/scikit-learn-real/hgb-repro/hgb-repro.log) is its output (scikit-learn 1.9.1, numpy 2.5).

### Expected Results

Training loss that does not increase for dozens of iterations at default settings, as with LightGBM/XGBoost at equivalent settings.

### Actual Results

`25: 0.4847, 50: 0.4380, (min 0.4180 @ 55), 100: 1.0845, 200: 1.9335`

### What makes it go away (one change at a time)

- **Fixes it:** `l2_regularization` ≥ 0.01; `min_hessian_to_split` ≥ 0.01 (patched into `TreeGrower`, as it isn't an estimator parameter); `learning_rate=0.05`; a zero baseline instead of the log class priors; **`min_samples_leaf=1`**.
- **Does not fix it:** `max_leaf_nodes` 7, 15 or 255 (255 is worst); `min_samples_leaf` 5 or 100; `min_hessian_to_split=0.002`. `learning_rate=0.2` makes it worse.

At `min_samples_leaf=1`, sklearn and LightGBM agree (0.155 vs 0.152 at iteration 200). At 5 and 20, only sklearn diverges. A likely reason: LightGBM checks `min_data_in_leaf` against bin counts *estimated from hessians* (`cnt_factor = num_data / sum_hessian` in `feature_histogram.hpp`), while sklearn uses true counts. sklearn can therefore build ~20–40-row leaves whose hessian sum is barely above `min_hessian_to_split=1e-3`. In the first rising iteration (20), one such leaf has 34 rows, G = 2.0, H = 1.05e-3 and a step of −191. That is my reading of the evidence, not a verified root cause.

With the default `early_stopping='auto'`, the fit stops at `n_iter_=11` (training loss 0.64), with leaf values already at 1.9e3.

Possible remedies: a documentation note on `l2_regularization`/`min_samples_leaf` for multiclass; a small non-zero default `l2_regularization` (XGBoost defaults to `lambda=1`); or exposing `min_hessian_to_split`.

### Versions

scikit-learn 1.9.1, numpy 2.5.4, scipy 1.18.1, Python 3.14 (conda-forge), on linux-aarch64 and linux-64. Results are identical on both.

> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Foreword

I am opening this to a few ideas I have in the back of my mind. Any kind of comments, feed-back, suggestions or help on this would be more than welcome!

The pain points this issue is trying to address are not well-defined and multi-factorial, but my hope is that we can identify smaller problems that can be addressed and that contribute to maintaining the project being a more pleasant experience.

As an example of super useful automation, the rule to auto-close PRs fixing an issue which has "Needs Triage" label https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/34506 by @virchan. We need more of this kind of things!

I am completely aware that some problems are on the human interaction side and can not be fixed by technological means. I am also well aware of the caveat of working on automation for the sake of automation and forgetting that it should help making the project more maintainable. If I put an idea below it's because I thought about it a bit and think it's worth doing it. Of course, you may disagree with me, and I would be happy to hear your objections!

cc @scikit-learn/core-devs @scikit-learn/contributor-experience-team 

### Add a few automated labels to make it easier to filter issues

In an ideal world GitHub would have this kind of features built-in but it doesn't 😓, trust me I double-checked 😉.

- PR diff size labels: #35142. PR diff size is an imperfect but good enough proxy to estimate how much time/energy a PR takes to review/merge. It's complementary to the "Quick review" label that is set manually.
- TODO number of approval labels. I envisage a label `review:one-approval`, `review:two-approvals`. One tweak would be that Contributor Experience Team members approvals are counted. Optionally a `review:ongoing` as soon as someone did a review, so that we can try to remember to follow-up.
- TODO contributor type of labels: `first-time-contributor`, `early-contributor` (less than 10 PRs merged), `seasoned-contributor` (more than 10 PR merged), `team-member`. This would be convenient to be able to filter between different modes of reviews rather than going to the default PR page, being driven by notifications, or other semi-random factors ...

One useful follow-up once we have these labels is to create additional [Views](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/views) to use them more easily.

### Add profile information to issue/PRs automatically to help dealing with automated accounts

The first thing is to show a summary of the profile information. We can discuss later about acting on it, like auto-closing the issue/PR, blocking the account, but let's first start by making the info easily accessible.

Tools that already exist:

- **AgentScan** they have an action used by plenty of "popular" projects, like [Node.js](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/main/.github/workflows/contributor-guidance.yml), [StoryBook](https://github.com/storybookjs/storybook/blob/next/.github/workflows/agent-scan.yml), [Vite](https://github.com/vitejs/vite/blob/main/.github/workflows/bot.yml). This is the first thing I use these days to do a [user scan](https://agentscan.tools/user/rxchitrx). There is also a [scikit-learn repo scan](https://agentscan.tools/scan/scikit-learn/scikit-learn) but less useful. In my experience, AgentScan is a bit too "nice" in the sense that I have seen accounts labeled as "organic", although it was a clear block for me, like 5-10 PRs opened in unrelated repos in the same day or so. 
- **[Anti slop](https://github.com/peakoss/anti-slop)**: used by "popular" projects like [HuggingFace Transformers](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/main/.github/workflows/anti-slop.yml) see [automated comment](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/pull/49621#issuecomment-6183948893). It's more a list of "simple rules" to check to avoid common patterns.
- **gh-profiler**: nice little tool but a bit limited. This is where I got the idea from showing the profile info in issues/PRs. For completeness, I opened an issue about tweaking the gh-profiler format and didn't get any reply so far [^1] https://github.com/ehmatthes/gh-profiler/issues/153.

[^1]: which is completely fine of course, we are all busy open-source maintainers

### Miscellaneous and not fully decided ideas

- rule to have early contributors (less than 10 PRs merged) open an issue before opening a PR? This adds a bit of latency in the system which I think is a good thing, even if it is a bit sad in a way that we have to do it ...

body_text: > [!WARNING] > This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label. In some cases sklearn breaks up work using `gen_even_slices()`. The typical number of slices is `n_jobs`. Here's an example from KNeighbors: ```python chunked_results = Parallel(n_jobs, prefer="threads")( delayed(self._tree.query)(X[s], n_neighbors, return_distance) for s in gen_even_slices(X.shape[0], n_jobs) ) ``` If each slice takes the exact amount of time, this is fine. ## The problem ### Uneven workloads mean reduced parallelism However, what happens if one slice takes longer to process? Since there is one slice per thread, the other threads will sit idle. That means effective parallelism is lower than requested parallelism. And in fact this happens with KNeighbors in some cases. Here's a sample profile ([original](https://share.firefox.dev/4iaYnwC)): Notice how most of the threads just sit idle towards the end. ### The solution: smaller chunks of work If you split up the input array into a larger number of smaller chunks, e.g. `n_jobs * 30`, you end up with much smaller holes of idleness at the end. That means higher effective parallelism. And then as long as the number of chunks isn't too large to start hitting the overhead of scheduling a task, you end up with faster results. ## Places where this might be the case If workload times are exactly proportional to input size, splitting up into more slices isn't necessary. So each case would need to be benchmarked separately. I'm pretty sure KNeighbors benefits, at minimum. ``` sklearn/decomposition/_lda.py 463: for idx_slice in gen_even_slices(X.shape[0], n_jobs) sklearn/decomposition/_dict_learning.py 444: slices = list(gen_even_slices(n_samples, effective_n_jobs(n_jobs))) sklearn/metrics/pairwise.py 1970: for s in gen_even_slices(_num_samples(Y), effective_n_jobs(n_jobs)) sklearn/neighbors/_base.py 912: for s in gen_even_slices(X.shape[0], n_jobs) 1269: for s in gen_even_slices(X.shape[0], n_jobs) ```

Currently, `move_estimator_to` will happily accept any estimator and silently move its public attributes to the requested namespace regardless of whether the resulting output will be usable or not.

Currently, there is a tag for array API support, but it appears to be based on whether `.fit()` will work only, while it is possible to successfully move and call prediction methods on cases that were fitted with parameters not covered by array API.

For instance, this works:
```python
import os
os.environ["SCIPY_ARRAY_API"] = "1"

from sklearn import set_config
set_config(array_api_dispatch=True)

import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=123)
X = rng.standard_normal(size=(20, 3))
y = rng.standard_normal(size=X.shape[0])

from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
model = LinearRegression(positive=True).fit(X, y)

import array_api_strict
from sklearn.utils._array_api import get_namespace_and_device, move_to, move_estimator_to
xp, _, device = get_namespace_and_device(array_api_strict.zeros(1))
model_moved = move_estimator_to(model, xp=xp, device=device)
X_moved = move_to(X, xp=xp, device=device)

model_moved.predict(X_moved)
```

### Describe your issue.

I observed that, for NumPy float64 arrays without NaNs, the p-value of an untied slice returned by `mannwhitneyu` with `method='auto'` and `axis=-1` depends on whether another slice contains ties.

Here, ties mean repeated values within the pooled pair of samples for an individual slice, not equal values appearing in different slices.

When either sample size is at most 8, the implementation I inspected chooses `exact` or `asymptotic` for the entire call based on whether any slice contains ties. Consequently, replacing separate calls in a loop with a single call using `axis` can change a slice's p-value even though that slice's own inputs have not changed.

I expected each slice's result to agree with a separate call. This expectation is related to the multidimensional input support discussed in [gh-12837](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/12837) and [gh-11113](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/11113), but I would like to clarify whether it also applies to automatic method selection.

For the untied target slice below, using a two-sided test with continuity correction enabled, U is 5:

```python
x = [0, 1, 2, 3, 9]
y = [4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10, 11]
```

| Call | Target slice's p-value |
| --- | --- |
| Alone, `method='auto'` | `0.04797979797979798` |
| Batched with another untied slice, `method='auto'` | `0.04797979797979798` |
| Batched with a slice containing one tied pair, `method='auto'` | `0.05131990358807116` |
| Alone, `method='exact'` | `0.04797979797979798` |
| Alone, `method='asymptotic'` | `0.05131990358807116` |

The target slice's inputs, sample sizes, and U are unchanged. The p-value crosses 0.05, changing this slice's decision at the 5% significance level. Reversing the rows of the batched input does not change the target slice's result. No multiple-testing correction is applied.

This behavior was observed with both SciPy `1.18.1` and development build `2.0.0.dev0+git20260902.fb96fc6`, with NumPy `2.3.5` at runtime in both environments.

For the untied target slice, enumerating all 792 rank allocations gives an inclusive two-sided exact probability of `38/792 = 19/396`. A separate implementation of the continuity-corrected normal approximation also agrees with the asymptotic value above. Both p-values are therefore consistent with their respective methods in this example. The concern is the choice of method for a slice changing because another slice contains ties, rather than an arithmetic error in the approximation.

In the inspected source, the method is selected by:

```python
_mwu_choose_method(n1, n2, xp.any(t > 1))
```

Because `xp.any(t > 1)` reduces over all axes, a tie in any slice selects `asymptotic` for the entire call. The asymptotic tie correction, however, is computed separately for each slice:

```python
xp.sum(t**3 - t, axis=-1)
```

This distinguishes the observed method-selection effect from another slice's tie correction being incorporated into the target slice's variance. The target slice's p-value in the mixed batch agrees with its standalone `method='asymptotic'` result.

It was not clear to me whether the docstring's “there are no ties” refers to each slice or the entire input. The latter interpretation would be consistent with the implementation.

In the tests I inspected, `test_gh_12837_11113` compares batched and separate calls but parametrizes only `exact` and `asymptotic`; `test_auto` uses one-dimensional inputs. Testing this case requires an explicit mixture of tied and untied slices, rather than just adding `auto` to the existing method parametrization.

A similar global tie check appears in the historical implementation in [gh-4933](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/4933). I have not checked every intervening version, so this is not an exhaustive regression analysis. I did not find a report directly addressing this cross-slice p-value dependency within the tracker material I reviewed.

For context, the Wilcoxon discussion in [gh-21567](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/21567) notes that `nan_policy='omit'` can produce different sample sizes across slices, allowing `auto` to choose different methods. That concerns a different test and input condition; I do not take it as defining the intended Mann–Whitney U behavior here.

**Question**

Is selecting one method for all slices based on ties anywhere in the input intentional?

- If so, could the `method` docstring explicitly explain that ties in another slice can change the selected method and p-value? Guidance on choosing an appropriate method for each slice would also help users who need agreement with separate calls. I am not suggesting applying `method='exact'` indiscriminately to tied slices, since it does not correct for ties.
- If per-slice automatic selection is the intended behavior, a test comparing separate and batched calls with an explicit mixture of tied and untied slices would cover this case.

I am not proposing a particular implementation. I have not measured how often this occurs in practice or its effects on Type I or Type II error rates.

**AI assistance**

I wrote the outline, drafted the text in Japanese, developed and executed the reproducer, performed the mathematical cross-checks, and inspected the source code and tracker myself. AI assistance was used only to translate the Japanese draft into English.

### Reproducing Code Example

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import mannwhitneyu

# Target slice A: no ties within the pooled sample.
x = np.array([0, 1, 2, 3, 9], dtype=np.float64)
y = np.array([4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10, 11], dtype=np.float64)

# Companion slice B: initially untied.
bx = x + 20
by = y + 20
bx_tied = bx.copy()
bx_tied[1] = bx_tied[0]  # Introduce one tied pair within B only.

options = dict(
    axis=-1,
    alternative="two-sided",
    use_continuity=True,
    nan_policy="propagate",
)

single = mannwhitneyu(x, y, method="auto", **options)
untied_batch = mannwhitneyu(
    np.stack([x, bx]), np.stack([y, by]), method="auto", **options
)
mixed_batch = mannwhitneyu(
    np.stack([x, bx_tied]), np.stack([y, by]), method="auto", **options
)
exact = mannwhitneyu(x, y, method="exact", **options)
asymptotic = mannwhitneyu(x, y, method="asymptotic", **options)
reversed_batch = mannwhitneyu(
    np.stack([bx_tied, x]), np.stack([by, y]), method="auto", **options
)

# Report A only; A is the second row in reversed_batch.
print("single auto:", single.statistic, single.pvalue)
print("untied batch A:", untied_batch.statistic[0], untied_batch.pvalue[0])
print("mixed batch A:", mixed_batch.statistic[0], mixed_batch.pvalue[0])
print("single exact:", exact.statistic, exact.pvalue)
print("single asymptotic:", asymptotic.statistic, asymptotic.pvalue)
print("reversed mixed batch A:", reversed_batch.statistic[1], reversed_batch.pvalue[1])
```

### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

After working on PR #26168 #26141 #25862 #26078 #25638 #25570 and a conversation with @ev-br , these features were either needed or would make sense to have in SciPy. This is a tracker issue _(for discussions and tracking the implementation)_ and one line explanation of why they may be needed.

### Describe the solution you'd like.

- [ ] P-spline penalties, a cheaper discrete alternative to the exact integral penalty
- [ ] Higher order derivative penalties (penalize the third derivative instead of the second)
- [ ] A `solver=` option to pick the linear algebra backend for the fitting problem
- [x] Wrap LAPACK `dpbcon` in `scipy.linalg` for a cheap condition number estimate from the Cholesky factor (and `?lansb`)
- [ ] Add `clamp_values` kwarg for `scipy.interpolate.make_smoothing_spline`
- [ ] Add splines with higher degree polynomials (`k > 3`)
- [ ] Support `periodic` smoothing splines
- [ ] Support batched `y` in a smoothing spline fit


### Describe alternatives you've considered.

_No response_

### Additional context (e.g. screenshots, GIFs)

1. P-Splines are very common in interpolation and are often used instead of smoothing splines.
2. Higher order derivatives are important for users that care about curvature. This was first requested in [#24532](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/24532).
3. A `solver=` param was first discussed [here](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/23472#issuecomment-3195872227). 
4. Smoothing parameter `lam` increases the `condition-number` proportionally, wrapping `dpbcon` in `scipy.linalg` would help estimate when the system becomes ill-posed instead of estimating it (which is the current behavior).
5. `scipy.interpolate.make_smoothing_spline` at `lam=0` is just a `make_lsq_spline`. Since lsq splines now support a `clamp_values` kwarg, it may be reasonable to add the same for smoothing splines.
6. Quartic and higher splines were first requested [here](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/24532).
